# Foundational NeRF: A Continuous 5D Radiance Field with Differentiable Volume Rendering

## Abstract

Foundational NeRF represents one scene as a continuous coordinate-based MLP field mapping 3D position and viewing direction to emitted RGB color and volume density. Density depends on position alone, supporting view-consistent occupancy and occlusion, while color may depend on viewing direction to represent view-dependent appearance. Camera rays are evaluated at sampled points, and differentiable emission-absorption volume rendering composites local colors using interval opacity and accumulated transmittance. Photometric loss between rendered and observed pixels, with known poses, back-propagates through this quadrature to optimize the MLP. Positional encoding and coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling are practical components that improve high-frequency detail and allocate more samples to contributing ray segments, but the baseline remains a per-scene continuous neural field rather than an explicit mesh, voxel model, or feed-forward reconstructor. ## Introduction

This review groups the foundational NeRF pipeline around three linked choices rather than treating every later NeRF variant as the same method: the scene representation, the ray-based rendering operator, and the image-supervised optimization loop. The scope here is the original NeRF formulation for novel view synthesis: learn a continuous volumetric scene function from posed photographs and render new camera views by integrating density and color along rays. Later systems that bake fields into voxels, polygons, meshes, hash grids, or other acceleration structures address efficiency, scale, aliasing, editing, or deployment objectives and should not be conflated with the baseline representation. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:01320e9d4bc0] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f]

At the representation level, NeRF defines a scene as a continuous 5D vector-valued function. Its input is a 3D spatial location x=(x,y,z) and a viewing direction, written in the original paper as (θ,φ) and implemented as a 3D Cartesian unit vector d; its output is an emitted RGB color c=(r,g,b) and a volume density σ. A multilayer perceptron FΘ approximates the mapping (x,d)→(c,σ), with separate treatment of geometry and appearance: density is predicted from position alone, while color may depend on both position and viewing direction. This design encourages multiview-consistent occupancy while allowing view-dependent appearance such as specular effects. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a]

For rendering, NeRF casts a camera ray r(t)=o+td and evaluates the network at sample locations along that ray. Classical volume rendering accumulates the samples into a pixel color: each sample contributes its color weighted by its local opacity, (1−exp(−σ_iδ_i)), and by accumulated transmittance T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jδ_j), where δ_i is the distance between adjacent samples. The resulting discrete sum is Ĉ(r)=Σ_i T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i))c_i, with a background term when ray termination is modeled. This quadrature is a piecewise-constant approximation to the continuous emission-absorption integral and is differentiable, so gradients from rendered pixels can update the MLP weights. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a]

Training therefore requires only images and known camera poses in the original setup: NeRF renders rays from the training viewpoints, compares predicted colors with observed pixel colors, and back-propagates the rendering loss through the compositing and network evaluations. The original method also uses positional encoding to expose high-frequency coordinate variation and a coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling strategy: a coarse network estimates sample weights, and a fine network receives additional samples drawn from the normalized coarse weights so that more evaluations concentrate where the ray is expected to contribute. These components make the foundational model a per-scene optimized continuous field, not a generic mesh or an explicit voxel reconstruction. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54]

## Background and Method Taxonomy

For this review, the organizing choice is a pipeline-based grouping: representation, rendering operator, and optimization objective. This grouping is used to explain the foundational NeRF formulation; it is not a universal taxonomy of all neural-rendering methods, nor is it a paper-proposed classification. Under this grouping, the defining relationship is that a continuous field supplies density and color at queried coordinates, differentiable volume rendering composites those samples along camera rays, and the resulting pixel error supervises the field. Later methods can still be NeRF-like if they preserve this field-to-ray-compositing relationship, even when they change the data structure or sampling strategy. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06]

The first classification criterion is what represents the scene. The original NeRF uses a per-scene, coordinate-based MLP: the network parameters encode a continuous function over 3D position and viewing direction rather than storing colors on an explicit mesh or a fixed voxel grid. This separates it from representations whose primary scene store is polygons, textured meshes, voxel textures, hash tables, sparse tensors, or other explicit feature structures. Such structures may be used to accelerate, bake, distill, or rasterize a NeRF-derived model, but they are different implementation choices from the original continuous MLP field. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce]

The second criterion is how geometry and appearance are factorized within the representation. In foundational NeRF, density is constrained to be a function of position only, whereas emitted RGB color can depend on position and viewing direction. That distinction is important: density supplies the view-invariant occupancy used by transmittance and occlusion, while directional color permits non-Lambertian or specular appearance. Methods that replace the view-dependent color shader with diffuse texture plus residuals, surface texture plus view-aware lobes, reflection-ray tracing, or learned feature decoding alter the appearance model; they should not be read as changing the original density-color distinction by itself. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54] [E:arxiv:2311.09806:abstract:claim:2225f1f6f32b]

The third criterion is the rendering integral and its discretization. Foundational NeRF casts one ray through each pixel, queries the field at points along that ray, and alpha-composites colors using local opacity and accumulated transmittance. This is emission-absorption volume rendering, not direct z-buffered surface rendering. A method that rasterizes textured polygons or mesh primitives and then invokes a small shader changes the primary visibility mechanism, even if it retains view-dependent color or was trained from a NeRF. Conversely, mip-NeRF remains closely related to the original ray-based formulation but replaces infinitesimal ray samples with anti-aliased conical frustums to encode scale, addressing blur and aliasing rather than replacing volume compositing with rasterization. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe]

The fourth criterion is sampling scope. Hierarchical volume sampling in the original NeRF is an efficiency allocation mechanism inside the same rendering formulation: a coarse network evaluates stratified samples, its normalized compositing weights define a piecewise-constant distribution, and inverse-transform sampling adds fine samples in regions expected to affect the pixel. The fine result still uses volume rendering over the union of samples. This differs from deployment-oriented acceleration schemes that bake the field, use deferred shaders, rasterize polygons, employ explicit level-of-detail structures, or partition large scenes; those change storage, hardware use, or visibility computation, whereas coarse-to-fine sampling changes where the MLP is queried. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719] [E:arxiv:2310.13263:abstract:claim:d66087edc431]

The final criterion is supervision and applicability. The original setup optimizes one scene from multiple posed images by comparing rendered and observed colors; it does not require explicit 3D labels in that formulation. Feed-forward or conditional NeRFs, single-image reconstruction systems, and generative diffusion-coupled methods introduce learned priors or additional conditioning and therefore solve a different data-regime problem from the original per-scene optimization. Likewise, methods focused on multiscale anti-aliasing, mobile frame rate, urban scale, geometry extraction, editing, or architecture conversion are related along selected pipeline dimensions but have distinct objectives; their results cannot be treated as direct rankings unless datasets, hardware, training views, and metrics are matched. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:42d03ceacbbb] [E:arxiv:2302.10109:abstract:claim:370fdae62ed9]

## Representative Methods

The foundational NeRF method represents one scene with a coordinate-based multilayer perceptron rather than an explicit mesh, voxel array, or point cloud. The network is a continuous 5D scene function FΘ(x,d)→(c,σ): x is a 3D position, d is the viewing direction represented in implementation as a three-dimensional Cartesian unit vector, c is emitted RGB color, and σ is volume density. Thus, every queried point in the scene volume returns local appearance and opacity-like density; the learned weights Θ are optimized for that scene from posed images. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] Geometry and appearance are deliberately factorized inside the MLP. Density is restricted to depend only on 3D position x, so the same spatial location has one occupancy field across viewpoints. Color is allowed to depend on both x and viewing direction d, which gives the model a mechanism for view-dependent non-Lambertian appearance such as specular highlights. In the original architecture, eight fully connected ReLU layers with 256 channels process position and output σ plus a 256-dimensional feature; that feature is concatenated with the ray direction and passed through an additional fully connected ReLU layer with 128 channels to predict RGB. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54]

A camera ray is written as r(t)=o+td, with origin o and unit direction d. NeRF evaluates the field at coordinates sampled along this ray and turns those local field values into one pixel color. This makes the representation volumetric: visibility is not decided by intersecting a single surface, but by accumulating emission and occlusion through the density distribution along the ray. The same ray-sampling procedure is used during training and novel-view rendering; only the camera pose and image pixels change. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] The continuous physical model is an emission-absorption volume integral. For a ray r(t), color is C(r)=∫ c(r(t),d) σ(r(t)) T(t) dt, where T(t)=exp(−∫_0^t σ(r(s))ds) is accumulated transmittance: the probability that light traveling from distance t toward the camera has not been stopped by earlier density. In this formulation, σ acts as an absorption coefficient or density field, while c is the radiance emitted at that location toward direction d. A finite far-boundary term can account for light entering from the background. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] NeRF approximates the integral numerically at N samples along each ray. If t_i is a sample, δ_i is the interval width to the next sample, σ_i and c_i are the network outputs at that sample, and T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jδ_j), then the discrete alpha-composited color is Ĉ(r)=Σ_{i=1}^{N} T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i))c_i, plus the background contribution weighted by remaining transmittance where used. The factor α_i=1−exp(−σ_iδ_i) is the local opacity assigned to the interval, while T_i is the product of earlier interval transmittances. This quadrature treats the field as approximately constant over each sampled neighborhood. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180]

Differentiability is the key property that connects rendering to representation learning. The sampled colors, densities, interval widths, transmittance products, and final pixel color form a computation graph through which a photometric rendering loss can be back-propagated to the MLP parameters. The original optimization compares colors rendered from training camera rays with observed ground-truth pixel colors; no explicit 3D geometry labels are required by this basic formulation. In other words, multi-view image consistency, mediated by known camera poses, supervises the continuous density and radiance function. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] The original implementation does not feed raw coordinates directly to the network in its high-frequency formulation. Positional encoding maps spatial and directional coordinates into sinusoidal features at multiple frequencies. This component addresses the difficulty that ordinary MLPs can have representing high-frequency color and geometry variation from low-dimensional coordinate inputs. It is therefore part of the practical NeRF mechanism for sharp view synthesis, but it is distinct from the density-color field definition and from the volume-rendering equation. [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:942ee00c2fdd]

Naive dense quadrature is expensive because the network is evaluated at many points along every pixel ray, including empty space and regions hidden behind visible content. Foundational NeRF therefore uses hierarchical volume sampling with two networks, called coarse and fine. The coarse network first evaluates N_c stratified samples along a ray. Its rendered color is rewritten as a weighted sum, with sample weights w_i=T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i)); after normalization, these weights define a piecewise-constant probability distribution over ray segments. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:297d1862724d] NeRF then draws N_f additional samples from the coarse distribution by inverse transform sampling and evaluates the fine network at the union of the original and second-stage samples. This places more network evaluations in segments that the coarse pass expects to contribute to the pixel, while still rendering the final color with the same differentiable volume-compositing equation over all N_c+N_f samples. The paper describes this as allocating samples according to expected effect rather than treating each sample as an independent Monte Carlo estimate of the whole integral. It is an internal sampling strategy, not a replacement of the continuous field with an explicit spatial data structure. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:297d1862724d]

The method’s contribution is therefore the combination of three ideas: a continuous 5D neural field with position-only density and directional color, classical differentiable volume rendering over ray samples, and pose-supervised per-scene optimization, made practical by positional encoding and coarse-to-fine sampling. The reported claim in the original paper is that this pipeline synthesizes novel views of complex scenes more faithfully than prior neural rendering and view-synthesis methods evaluated there. That evidence supports the original method’s role as a learned view-synthesis representation; it does not by itself establish fast rendering, explicit geometry extraction, or feed-forward reconstruction across scenes. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] The applicability boundary of foundational NeRF is narrower than that of the broader NeRF family. It optimizes a separate network for each scene, requires training images with known camera poses in the original setup, and renders by querying an MLP many times per ray. Consequently, later methods that condition a NeRF on input images, distill between MLP and explicit-grid architectures, bake features into voxels, rasterize polygons, trace reflection rays, or model surfaces and textures are modifying the data regime, representation store, rendering path, or appearance model; they should not be described as merely repeating the original 5D MLP and ray-marching mechanism. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:42d03ceacbbb] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f] Two later comparisons clarify what is and is not changed in the foundational formulation. Mip-NeRF retains the neural-field and anti-aliased volume-rendering lineage but queries conical frustums with integrated positional encoding so that scale-dependent blur and aliasing can be modeled; it targets a sampling limitation of one ray per pixel. MobileNeRF instead changes deployment-oriented visibility by representing a baked NeRF with textured polygons and using z-buffer rasterization followed by a small view-dependent MLP. These are related NeRF-derived systems, but neither is the same mechanism as the original continuous MLP evaluated at point samples along camera rays. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719]

## Comparative Evidence Analysis

The experimental comparison in this review is organized by the same pipeline dimensions used above—representation, ray-sampled differentiable rendering, and optimization—rather than by treating all later NeRF-derived systems as one benchmark family. The original NeRF evidence establishes that a per-scene MLP field, volume rendering, posed-image supervision, positional encoding, and hierarchical sampling can outperform the neural rendering and view-synthesis baselines evaluated in that paper. The selected later papers provide evidence about different objectives, such as anti-aliasing, deployment speed, architecture conversion, or surface rendering; their numbers are not a matched ranking against foundational NeRF unless dataset, task, hardware, views, and metrics are the same. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f] The foundational NeRF experiment is a novel-view-synthesis experiment: optimize a separate continuous 5D network for each scene from a sparse set of posed input images, render held-out camera rays by differentiable volume compositing, and compare rendered RGB pixels with ground-truth images. Its central quantitative claim in the source is state-of-the-art view synthesis on the complex scenes used in the original study. The frozen source excerpts supplied here do not include the paper's full per-dataset metric table, so this section should not invent PSNR, SSIM, or LPIPS values for the original benchmark. What is directly supported is the comparison direction and the evaluation mechanism, not an unstated numerical score. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:56629e322cde] Within the original method, the coarse and fine networks are compared under the same rendering equation but with different sample allocations. The coarse network evaluates N_c stratified samples and forms weights w_i=T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i)); normalized weights define a piecewise-constant PDF, inverse-transform sampling adds N_f samples, and the fine network renders from the union of N_c+N_f samples. This is therefore not a comparison between two unrelated rendering models: the fine stage uses the coarse stage's density-weighted estimate to place more queries in visible or otherwise contributing regions. The supported benefit is better allocation of ray samples; the excerpt does not provide a standalone coarse-versus-fine PSNR table. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:297d1862724d] The discrete rendering experiment also exposes the main cost dimension. Each pixel requires a camera ray, and each ray requires many MLP evaluations at sample positions; dense quadrature repeatedly queries free space and occluded regions that contribute little or nothing to the final color. Hierarchical sampling mitigates this waste inside NeRF by biasing later samples toward expected content, but it does not change the fundamental requirement of network evaluation along rays. Consequently, the original method's evidence supports high-quality offline view synthesis more directly than interactive rendering; later speed claims must be attributed to their changed representations or rendering pipelines. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719]

Mip-NeRF is the closest selected comparison on the rendering-sampling dimension because it preserves the neural radiance-field lineage but changes the query primitive from an infinitesimal point sample along a single ray to an anti-aliased conical frustum encoding continuous scale. On the dataset presented with NeRF, mip-NeRF is reported to reduce average error rates by 17% relative to NeRF; on a challenging multiscale variant introduced by mip-NeRF, the reduction is 60%. It is also reported to be about 7% faster than NeRF, half the size, and capable of matching brute-force supersampled NeRF accuracy on the multiscale dataset while being 22× faster. These results are specific to the scale/anti-aliasing setting and should not be generalized as ordinary fixed-resolution superiority. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:b14753cf9c18] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:section:abstract:3:97643459cce9:claim:4cdea39204ef] The mip-NeRF comparison also clarifies why supersampling is not an apples-to-apples baseline for interactive use. Casting multiple rays per pixel can reduce aliasing, but runtime generally scales with the supersampling rate because every extra ray still requires hundreds of MLP queries in NeRF. Mip-NeRF's reported 22× speed advantage is relative to brute-force supersampled NeRF on the authors' multiscale dataset, not relative to every explicit-grid or rasterization accelerator. Likewise, its 7% speed gain over NeRF and half-as-large model arise from integrating coarse and fine sampling into a single MLP in that system; they are not properties of the original coarse-plus-fine NeRF architecture. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:section:abstract:3:97643459cce9:claim:4cdea39204ef] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe]

A later multiscale system, Mip-VoG, addresses a different deployment point from mip-NeRF. It uses explicit multiscale mip voxel grids, ray-differential level-of-detail, quadrilinear interpolation across neighboring downsampled grids, a density grid, and a feature grid with a small MLP for view-dependent color. The authors state that mip-NeRF relies on integrated positional encoding and MLP queries and is therefore suited to offline rendering, whereas Mip-VoG targets simultaneous multiscale training and real-time anti-aliased rendering. Their reported result is superiority over state-of-the-art real-time rendering baselines on multiscale datasets; the supplied excerpt does not provide matched metric values or a direct head-to-head runtime table against original NeRF, so no numerical ranking can be reconstructed here. [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:3fee88baf342] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:8c68b6aea657] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:a6741b551651] Deployment-oriented methods change the primary visibility mechanism and therefore do not yield a like-for-like NeRF rendering-quality score. MobileNeRF represents a baked NeRF as textured polygons carrying binary opacities and feature vectors; z-buffer rasterization produces per-pixel features, and a small view-dependent MLP in a fragment shader decodes the final color. Its evidence targets interactive frame rates across commodity platforms, including mobile devices, by exploiting standard polygon rasterization rather than specialized ray marching. This comparison supports a hardware-pipeline and latency objective, but the selected excerpt does not supply a common dataset metric table against the original NeRF implementation. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:b57734e55004] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:72ae3e030d32] SNeRG illustrates the same distinction one step before MobileNeRF. It bakes NeRF into a sparse neural radiance grid in which active voxels store opacity, diffuse color, and a learned feature vector; ray marching first accumulates diffuse colors and features, and a lightweight deferred MLP converts the accumulated feature into a view-dependent residual. The source reports that this precomputation and deferred rendering increase NeRF rendering speed by three orders of magnitude, but also notes continued dependence on ray marching through a sparse voxel grid and substantial GPU memory for volumetric textures. Thus, the speed result is tied to baking and altered storage, not to the original MLP-only representation, and it comes with a memory trade-off. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:72ae3e030d32]

Architecture-conversion evidence is also distinct from view-synthesis benchmarking. PVD converts among MLP, sparse-tensor, low-rank-tensor, hash-table, and composite NeRF representations through progressive volume distillation, with special density handling for numerical stability. On NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF, and TanksAndTemples, the authors report that an MLP-based NeRF student distilled from a hash-table-based Instant-NGP teacher can be trained 10× to 20× faster than training the original NeRF from scratch while attaining superior synthesis quality. That comparison concerns post hoc representation conversion and training cost under PVD's distillation protocol; it does not show that an ordinary from-scratch MLP NeRF is intrinsically 10–20× slower than every other method or that quality is identical across all architecture pairs. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:538fa5305be2] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:4:97facdcc473c:claim:cec90d41fbf0] Across these selected studies, the comparable scientific conclusion is narrow and mechanism-based. The original NeRF's differentiable volume-rendering formulation enables image-based optimization of a continuous density-color field; hierarchical sampling improves sample allocation but retains many per-ray MLP queries. Mip-NeRF offers matched evidence for scale-aware frustum queries in multiscale anti-aliasing. Baked voxel, polygon, hash-grid, mesh-primitive, and distillation systems report speed, memory, platform, or conversion benefits after changing the storage or visibility pipeline. Because their tasks, datasets, baselines, hardware, and output objectives differ, the available excerpts do not support a single global ranking; the defensible comparison is that the foundational formulation is the common differentiable rendering baseline, while later numbers measure specific modifications under specific experimental conditions. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f]

## Limitations and Open Problems

The main computational limitation follows directly from the foundational rendering equation. NeRF must cast a ray for each pixel and evaluate an MLP at hundreds of sample positions along that ray to estimate and integrate density and radiance; free space and occluded regions can still be queried repeatedly. Coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling allocates more samples to segments expected to contribute, but it remains a ray-marching, multi-evaluation process rather than a constant-time surface lookup. The implication is that the original formulation is well matched to offline per-scene optimization and high-quality view synthesis, but its basic rendering path is too expensive for interactive visualization without changing sampling, storage, or the visibility pipeline. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719]

A second limitation is scale and aliasing. Foundational NeRF samples a scene with a single ray per pixel, so it can produce blurred results when training images observe content at nonuniform scales and aliasing or jagged artifacts when test views are distant. Simply casting multiple rays per pixel is a direct supersampling remedy, but in NeRF it multiplies an already large MLP-query cost and is generally impractical outside offline rendering. Mip-NeRF's scale-aware conical frustums and later explicit mip voxel grids are evidence that this is a real limitation of point-ray sampling; they also show that anti-aliasing and real-time deployment may require separate architectural changes. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:section:abstract:3:97643459cce9:claim:4cdea39204ef] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:3fee88baf342]

The continuous density field is a rendering representation, not by itself an unambiguous explicit surface reconstruction. NeRF is supervised through rendered color, and later analysis identifies a shape-radiance ambiguity: view-dependent radiance and inferred geometry can interact so that image fidelity does not necessarily determine one unique geometric explanation. This matters when the desired output is a mesh, accurate normals, animation, or manipulation rather than a novel-view image. Methods that normalize view dependence or use explicit surface and texture models target that geometry ambiguity, but they add assumptions or components not present in the original color-supervised volume-rendering setup. [E:arxiv:2010.07492:abstract:claim:a215bcfde7b2] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:249ec5b6f7a4] [E:arxiv:2311.09806:abstract:claim:2225f1f6f32b]

View-dependent color is both a capability and a modeling boundary. Allowing RGB to depend on position and viewing direction lets foundational NeRF represent non-Lambertian effects such as specular highlights, but highly shiny scenes can contain quickly changing appearance and reflections of nearby content that a single outgoing-radiance MLP may model only at substantial network cost. Reflection-ray methods address this by tracing additional rays through the field and decoding traced features with a smaller network. That evidence should be read as a limitation of the original appearance model under strong specularity, not as a failure of density-based volume rendering in general. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2405.14871:abstract:claim:1aed0f9d756b] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54]

The original NeRF also has a data-regime limitation: it optimizes a separate MLP for each scene from posed training images. It is not a feed-forward model that reconstructs an unseen scene from one image, and the basic formulation assumes camera poses are available for photometric supervision. PixelNeRF and conditional or diffusion-distilled systems introduce image features, learned cross-scene priors, or generated virtual views to operate from one or a sparse set of inputs. These methods relax the original data requirement, but they change the learning problem and should not be interpreted as the same per-scene optimization result. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:42d03ceacbbb] [E:arxiv:2302.10109:abstract:claim:370fdae62ed9]

Memory and hardware compatibility create a separate trade-off when NeRFs are accelerated. Caching or baking a continuous field into sparse voxels can improve rendering speed, but it raises storage or GPU-memory use; SNeRG's precomputed sparse grid, for example, accelerates deferred rendering yet still ray-marches volumetric textures and requires significant GPU memory. MobileNeRF instead moves visibility to textured polygons and z-buffer rasterization so commodity graphics pipelines and mobile GPUs can be used. These are deployment solutions, not free speedups of the original MLP: they alter the representation store and often require baking or a deferred shader. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:72ae3e030d32] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce]

Large scenes intensify both computation and organization costs. A single monolithic ray-marched field does not naturally map to the culling, level-of-detail, and rasterization mechanisms used for urban-scale interactive graphics. Systems such as UE4-NeRF partition scenes and combine optimized mesh-like proxies with game-engine rasterization, while deformable neural mesh primitives seek rasterization efficiency and lower peak memory for urban rendering. Their speed and memory claims depend on those primitives, partitioning, level-of-detail, and engine integration; they do not establish that the unmodified foundational NeRF has the same scalability. [E:arxiv:2310.13263:abstract:claim:d66087edc431] [E:arxiv:2307.10776:abstract:claim:e4c55e718898] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719]

Architecture choice also involves downstream trade-offs beyond average rendering quality. Plain MLPs provide a continuous coordinate field with comparatively clear functional structure, whereas hash tables, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, tri-planes, and hybrid encodings can train or render faster but may have less clear geometric meaning or different memory profiles. PVD's any-to-any distillation and Hyb-NeRF's coarse-to-fine hybrid encoding are responses to this fragmentation: practitioners may convert or combine representations for editing, training speed, rendering speed, or memory. The limitation is that no single store in the selected evidence dominates all of these objectives simultaneously. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:4:97facdcc473c:claim:cec90d41fbf0] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:95df0ad0b144]

The physical scope of the basic emission-absorption model should also be distinguished from full participating-media light transport. The NeRF integral accumulates locally emitted color and density along a camera ray; it does not, in its foundational form, solve multiple scattering or global illumination in a general volumetric medium. Work on volumetric clouds uses a physically based differentiable volume renderer and diffusion prior to provide gradients for multiple-scattering light transport, explicitly contrasting that setting with classic NeRF approaches. Thus, strong scattering media are outside the applicability boundary of the original local radiance-and-density formulation. [E:arxiv:2501.05226:abstract:claim:c3f096e7de3c] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a]

Taken together, these limitations should be attributed to specific parts of the pipeline rather than used as a blanket claim that neural radiance fields are unsuitable. The original formulation's core open trade-offs are: many MLP evaluations per ray, point-sample aliasing under scale change, geometry ambiguity under photometric and view-dependent supervision, per-scene posed-image training, and difficulty matching commodity rasterization hardware without baking or restructuring the field. Later evidence shows that anti-aliasing, feed-forward priors, surface models, reflection tracing, explicit grids, polygons, mesh primitives, and architecture distillation can address individual constraints, but each changes assumptions and introduces its own quality, memory, physical-accuracy, editing, or deployment trade-off. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f]

## Conclusion

The core answer is that NeRF combines a 5D neural radiance field with classical differentiable volume rendering: the MLP supplies density and color at queried ray coordinates, transmittance-weighted alpha compositing forms each pixel, and posed-image error supervises the field without explicit 3D labels. The discrete estimator is Ĉ(r)=Σ_i T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i))c_i, with optional remaining-transmittance background weighting. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180]

The main trade-off is expressive, image-based view synthesis against sampling cost: hierarchical sampling concentrates MLP evaluations where coarse weights indicate contribution, but the original method still requires many network queries per ray and is best understood as offline per-scene optimization. Its point-ray formulation also leaves scale aliasing, geometry ambiguity, and deployment acceleration to later modified architectures rather than being solved by the baseline representation itself. report.html:
Foundational NeRF: A Continuous 5D Radiance Field with Differentiable Volume Rendering

Abstract

Foundational NeRF represents one scene as a continuous coordinate-based MLP field mapping 3D position and viewing direction to emitted RGB color and volume density. Density depends on position alone, supporting view-consistent occupancy and occlusion, while color may depend on viewing direction to represent view-dependent appearance. Camera rays are evaluated at sampled points, and differentiable emission-absorption volume rendering composites local colors using interval opacity and accumulated transmittance. Photometric loss between rendered and observed pixels, with known poses, back-propagates through this quadrature to optimize the MLP. Positional encoding and coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling are practical components that improve high-frequency detail and allocate more samples to contributing ray segments, but the baseline remains a per-scene continuous neural field rather than an explicit mesh, voxel model, or feed-forward reconstructor. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:942ee00c2fdd] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:297d1862724d]

Introduction

This review groups the foundational NeRF pipeline around three linked choices rather than treating every later NeRF variant as the same method: the scene representation, the ray-based rendering operator, and the image-supervised optimization loop. The scope here is the original NeRF formulation for novel view synthesis: learn a continuous volumetric scene function from posed photographs and render new camera views by integrating density and color along rays. Later systems that bake fields into voxels, polygons, meshes, hash grids, or other acceleration structures address efficiency, scale, aliasing, editing, or deployment objectives and should not be conflated with the baseline representation. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:01320e9d4bc0] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f]

At the representation level, NeRF defines a scene as a continuous 5D vector-valued function. Its input is a 3D spatial location x=(x,y,z) and a viewing direction, written in the original paper as (θ,φ) and implemented as a 3D Cartesian unit vector d; its output is an emitted RGB color c=(r,g,b) and a volume density σ. A multilayer perceptron FΘ approximates the mapping (x,d)→(c,σ), with separate treatment of geometry and appearance: density is predicted from position alone, while color may depend on both position and viewing direction. This design encourages multiview-consistent occupancy while allowing view-dependent appearance such as specular effects. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a]

For rendering, NeRF casts a camera ray r(t)=o+td and evaluates the network at sample locations along that ray. Classical volume rendering accumulates the samples into a pixel color: each sample contributes its color weighted by its local opacity, (1−exp(−σ_iδ_i)), and by accumulated transmittance T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jδ_j), where δ_i is the distance between adjacent samples. The resulting discrete sum is Ĉ(r)=Σ_i T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i))c_i, with a background term when ray termination is modeled. This quadrature is a piecewise-constant approximation to the continuous emission-absorption integral and is differentiable, so gradients from rendered pixels can update the MLP weights. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a]

Training therefore requires only images and known camera poses in the original setup: NeRF renders rays from the training viewpoints, compares predicted colors with observed pixel colors, and back-propagates the rendering loss through the compositing and network evaluations. The original method also uses positional encoding to expose high-frequency coordinate variation and a coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling strategy: a coarse network estimates sample weights, and a fine network receives additional samples drawn from the normalized coarse weights so that more evaluations concentrate where the ray is expected to contribute. These components make the foundational model a per-scene optimized continuous field, not a generic mesh or an explicit voxel reconstruction. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54]

Background and Method Taxonomy

For this review, the organizing choice is a pipeline-based grouping: representation, rendering operator, and optimization objective. This grouping is used to explain the foundational NeRF formulation; it is not a universal taxonomy of all neural-rendering methods, nor is it a paper-proposed classification. Under this grouping, the defining relationship is that a continuous field supplies density and color at queried coordinates, differentiable volume rendering composites those samples along camera rays, and the resulting pixel error supervises the field. Later methods can still be NeRF-like if they preserve this field-to-ray-compositing relationship, even when they change the data structure or sampling strategy. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06]

The first classification criterion is what represents the scene. The original NeRF uses a per-scene, coordinate-based MLP: the network parameters encode a continuous function over 3D position and viewing direction rather than storing colors on an explicit mesh or a fixed voxel grid. This separates it from representations whose primary scene store is polygons, textured meshes, voxel textures, hash tables, sparse tensors, or other explicit feature structures. Such structures may be used to accelerate, bake, distill, or rasterize a NeRF-derived model, but they are different implementation choices from the original continuous MLP field. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce]

The second criterion is how geometry and appearance are factorized within the representation. In foundational NeRF, density is constrained to be a function of position only, whereas emitted RGB color can depend on position and viewing direction. That distinction is important: density supplies the view-invariant occupancy used by transmittance and occlusion, while directional color permits non-Lambertian or specular appearance. Methods that replace the view-dependent color shader with diffuse texture plus residuals, surface texture plus view-aware lobes, reflection-ray tracing, or learned feature decoding alter the appearance model; they should not be read as changing the original density-color distinction by itself. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54] [E:arxiv:2311.09806:abstract:claim:2225f1f6f32b]

The third criterion is the rendering integral and its discretization. Foundational NeRF casts one ray through each pixel, queries the field at points along that ray, and alpha-composites colors using local opacity and accumulated transmittance. This is emission-absorption volume rendering, not direct z-buffered surface rendering. A method that rasterizes textured polygons or mesh primitives and then invokes a small shader changes the primary visibility mechanism, even if it retains view-dependent color or was trained from a NeRF. Conversely, mip-NeRF remains closely related to the original ray-based formulation but replaces infinitesimal ray samples with anti-aliased conical frustums to encode scale, addressing blur and aliasing rather than replacing volume compositing with rasterization. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe]

The fourth criterion is sampling scope. Hierarchical volume sampling in the original NeRF is an efficiency allocation mechanism inside the same rendering formulation: a coarse network evaluates stratified samples, its normalized compositing weights define a piecewise-constant distribution, and inverse-transform sampling adds fine samples in regions expected to affect the pixel. The fine result still uses volume rendering over the union of samples. This differs from deployment-oriented acceleration schemes that bake the field, use deferred shaders, rasterize polygons, employ explicit level-of-detail structures, or partition large scenes; those change storage, hardware use, or visibility computation, whereas coarse-to-fine sampling changes where the MLP is queried. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719] [E:arxiv:2310.13263:abstract:claim:d66087edc431]

The final criterion is supervision and applicability. The original setup optimizes one scene from multiple posed images by comparing rendered and observed colors; it does not require explicit 3D labels in that formulation. Feed-forward or conditional NeRFs, single-image reconstruction systems, and generative diffusion-coupled methods introduce learned priors or additional conditioning and therefore solve a different data-regime problem from the original per-scene optimization. Likewise, methods focused on multiscale anti-aliasing, mobile frame rate, urban scale, geometry extraction, editing, or architecture conversion are related along selected pipeline dimensions but have distinct objectives; their results cannot be treated as direct rankings unless datasets, hardware, training views, and metrics are matched. Representative Methods

The foundational NeRF method represents one scene with a coordinate-based multilayer perceptron rather than an explicit mesh, voxel array, or point cloud. The network is a continuous 5D scene function FΘ(x,d)→(c,σ): x is a 3D position, d is the viewing direction represented in implementation as a three-dimensional Cartesian unit vector, c is emitted RGB color, and σ is volume density. Thus, every queried point in the scene volume returns local appearance and opacity-like density; the learned weights Θ are optimized for that scene from posed images. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] Geometry and appearance are deliberately factorized inside the MLP. Density is restricted to depend only on 3D position x, so the same spatial location has one occupancy field across viewpoints. Color is allowed to depend on both x and viewing direction d, which gives the model a mechanism for view-dependent non-Lambertian appearance such as specular highlights. In the original architecture, eight fully connected ReLU layers with 256 channels process position and output σ plus a 256-dimensional feature; that feature is concatenated with the ray direction and passed through an additional fully connected ReLU layer with 128 channels to predict RGB. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54]

A camera ray is written as r(t)=o+td, with origin o and unit direction d. NeRF evaluates the field at coordinates sampled along this ray and turns those local field values into one pixel color. This makes the representation volumetric: visibility is not decided by intersecting a single surface, but by accumulating emission and occlusion through the density distribution along the ray. The same ray-sampling procedure is used during training and novel-view rendering; only the camera pose and image pixels change. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] The continuous physical model is an emission-absorption volume integral. For a ray r(t), color is C(r)=∫ c(r(t),d) σ(r(t)) T(t) dt, where T(t)=exp(−∫0^t σ(r(s))ds) is accumulated transmittance: the probability that light traveling from distance t toward the camera has not been stopped by earlier density. In this formulation, σ acts as an absorption coefficient or density field, while c is the radiance emitted at that location toward direction d. A finite far-boundary term can account for light entering from the background. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] NeRF approximates the integral numerically at N samples along each ray. If t_i is a sample, δ_i is the interval width to the next sample, σ_i and c_i are the network outputs at that sample, and T_i=exp(−Σ{j<i}σ_jδ_j), then the discrete alpha-composited color is Ĉ(r)=Σ_{i=1}^{N} T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i))c_i, plus the background contribution weighted by remaining transmittance where used. The factor α_i=1−exp(−σ_iδ_i) is the local opacity assigned to the interval, while T_i is the product of earlier interval transmittances. This quadrature treats the field as approximately constant over each sampled neighborhood. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180]

Differentiability is the key property that connects rendering to representation learning. The sampled colors, densities, interval widths, transmittance products, and final pixel color form a computation graph through which a photometric rendering loss can be back-propagated to the MLP parameters. The original optimization compares colors rendered from training camera rays with observed ground-truth pixel colors; no explicit 3D geometry labels are required by this basic formulation. In other words, multi-view image consistency, mediated by known camera poses, supervises the continuous density and radiance function. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] The original implementation does not feed raw coordinates directly to the network in its high-frequency formulation. Positional encoding maps spatial and directional coordinates into sinusoidal features at multiple frequencies. This component addresses the difficulty that ordinary MLPs can have representing high-frequency color and geometry variation from low-dimensional coordinate inputs. It is therefore part of the practical NeRF mechanism for sharp view synthesis, but it is distinct from the density-color field definition and from the volume-rendering equation. [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:942ee00c2fdd]

Naive dense quadrature is expensive because the network is evaluated at many points along every pixel ray, including empty space and regions hidden behind visible content. Foundational NeRF therefore uses hierarchical volume sampling with two networks, called coarse and fine. The coarse network first evaluates N_c stratified samples along a ray. Its rendered color is rewritten as a weighted sum, with sample weights w_i=T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i)); after normalization, these weights define a piecewise-constant probability distribution over ray segments. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:297d1862724d] NeRF then draws N_f additional samples from the coarse distribution by inverse transform sampling and evaluates the fine network at the union of the original and second-stage samples. This places more network evaluations in segments that the coarse pass expects to contribute to the pixel, while still rendering the final color with the same differentiable volume-compositing equation over all N_c+N_f samples. The paper describes this as allocating samples according to expected effect rather than treating each sample as an independent Monte Carlo estimate of the whole integral. It is an internal sampling strategy, not a replacement of the continuous field with an explicit spatial data structure. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:297d1862724d]

The method’s contribution is therefore the combination of three ideas: a continuous 5D neural field with position-only density and directional color, classical differentiable volume rendering over ray samples, and pose-supervised per-scene optimization, made practical by positional encoding and coarse-to-fine sampling. The reported claim in the original paper is that this pipeline synthesizes novel views of complex scenes more faithfully than prior neural rendering and view-synthesis methods evaluated there. That evidence supports the original method’s role as a learned view-synthesis representation; it does not by itself establish fast rendering, explicit geometry extraction, or feed-forward reconstruction across scenes. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] The applicability boundary of foundational NeRF is narrower than that of the broader NeRF family. It optimizes a separate network for each scene, requires training images with known camera poses in the original setup, and renders by querying an MLP many times per ray. Consequently, later methods that condition a NeRF on input images, distill between MLP and explicit-grid architectures, bake features into voxels, rasterize polygons, trace reflection rays, or model surfaces and textures are modifying the data regime, representation store, rendering path, or appearance model; they should not be described as merely repeating the original 5D MLP and ray-marching mechanism. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:42d03ceacbbb] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f] Two later comparisons clarify what is and is not changed in the foundational formulation. Mip-NeRF retains the neural-field and anti-aliased volume-rendering lineage but queries conical frustums with integrated positional encoding so that scale-dependent blur and aliasing can be modeled; it targets a sampling limitation of one ray per pixel. MobileNeRF instead changes deployment-oriented visibility by representing a baked NeRF with textured polygons and using z-buffer rasterization followed by a small view-dependent MLP. These are related NeRF-derived systems, but neither is the same mechanism as the original continuous MLP evaluated at point samples along camera rays. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719]

Comparative Evidence Analysis

The experimental comparison in this review is organized by the same pipeline dimensions used above—representation, ray-sampled differentiable rendering, and optimization—rather than by treating all later NeRF-derived systems as one benchmark family. The original NeRF evidence establishes that a per-scene MLP field, volume rendering, posed-image supervision, positional encoding, and hierarchical sampling can outperform the neural rendering and view-synthesis baselines evaluated in that paper. The selected later papers provide evidence about different objectives, such as anti-aliasing, deployment speed, architecture conversion, or surface rendering; their numbers are not a matched ranking against foundational NeRF unless dataset, task, hardware, views, and metrics are the same. Its central quantitative claim in the source is state-of-the-art view synthesis on the complex scenes used in the original study. The frozen source excerpts supplied here do not include the paper's full per-dataset metric table, so this section should not invent PSNR, SSIM, or LPIPS values for the original benchmark. What is directly supported is the comparison direction and the evaluation mechanism, not an unstated numerical score. The coarse network evaluates N_c stratified samples and forms weights w_i=T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i)); normalized weights define a piecewise-constant PDF, inverse-transform sampling adds N_f samples, and the fine network renders from the union of N_c+N_f samples. This is therefore not a comparison between two unrelated rendering models: the fine stage uses the coarse stage's density-weighted estimate to place more queries in visible or otherwise contributing regions. The supported benefit is better allocation of ray samples; the excerpt does not provide a standalone coarse-versus-fine PSNR table. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:297d1862724d] The discrete rendering experiment also exposes the main cost dimension. Each pixel requires a camera ray, and each ray requires many MLP evaluations at sample positions; dense quadrature repeatedly queries free space and occluded regions that contribute little or nothing to the final color. Hierarchical sampling mitigates this waste inside NeRF by biasing later samples toward expected content, but it does not change the fundamental requirement of network evaluation along rays. Consequently, the original method's evidence supports high-quality offline view synthesis more directly than interactive rendering; later speed claims must be attributed to their changed representations or rendering pipelines. Mip-NeRF is the closest selected comparison on the rendering-sampling dimension because it preserves the neural radiance-field lineage but changes the query primitive from an infinitesimal point sample along a single ray to an anti-aliased conical frustum encoding continuous scale. On the dataset presented with NeRF, mip-NeRF is reported to reduce average error rates by 17% relative to NeRF; on a challenging multiscale variant introduced by mip-NeRF, the reduction is 60%. It is also reported to be about 7% faster than NeRF, half the size, and capable of matching brute-force supersampled NeRF accuracy on the multiscale dataset while being 22× faster. Limitations and Open Problems

The main computational limitation follows directly from the foundational rendering equation. NeRF must cast a ray for each pixel and evaluate an MLP at hundreds of sample positions along that ray to estimate and integrate density and radiance; free space and occluded regions can still be queried repeatedly. Coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling allocates more samples to segments expected to contribute, but it remains a ray-marching, multi-evaluation process rather than a constant-time surface lookup. The implication is that the original formulation is well matched to offline per-scene optimization and high-quality view synthesis, but its basic rendering path is too expensive for interactive visualization without changing sampling, storage, or the visibility pipeline. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719]

A second limitation is scale and aliasing. Foundational NeRF samples a scene with a single ray per pixel, so it can produce blurred results when training images observe content at nonuniform scales and aliasing or jagged artifacts when test views are distant. Simply casting multiple rays per pixel is a direct supersampling remedy, but in NeRF it multiplies an already large MLP-query cost and is generally impractical outside offline rendering. Mip-NeRF's scale-aware conical frustums and later explicit mip voxel grids are evidence that this is a real limitation of point-ray sampling; they also show that anti-aliasing and real-time deployment may require separate architectural changes. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:section:abstract:3:97643459cce9:claim:4cdea39204ef] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:3fee88baf342]

The continuous density field is a rendering representation, not by itself an unambiguous explicit surface reconstruction. NeRF is supervised through rendered color, and later analysis identifies a shape-radiance ambiguity: view-dependent radiance and inferred geometry can interact so that image fidelity does not necessarily determine one unique geometric explanation. This matters when the desired output is a mesh, accurate normals, animation, or manipulation rather than a novel-view image. Methods that normalize view dependence or use explicit surface and texture models target that geometry ambiguity, but they add assumptions or components not present in the original color-supervised volume-rendering setup. [E:arxiv:2010.07492:abstract:claim:a215bcfde7b2] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:249ec5b6f7a4] [E:arxiv:2311.09806:abstract:claim:2225f1f6f32b]

View-dependent color is both a capability and a modeling boundary. Allowing RGB to depend on position and viewing direction lets foundational NeRF represent non-Lambertian effects such as specular highlights, but highly shiny scenes can contain quickly changing appearance and reflections of nearby content that a single outgoing-radiance MLP may model only at substantial network cost. Reflection-ray methods address this by tracing additional rays through the field and decoding traced features with a smaller network. That evidence should be read as a limitation of the original appearance model under strong specularity, not as a failure of density-based volume rendering in general. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2405.14871:abstract:claim:1aed0f9d756b] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54]

The original NeRF also has a data-regime limitation: it optimizes a separate MLP for each scene from posed training images. It is not a feed-forward model that reconstructs an unseen scene from one image, and the basic formulation assumes camera poses are available for photometric supervision. PixelNeRF and conditional or diffusion-distilled systems introduce image features, learned cross-scene priors, or generated virtual views to operate from one or a sparse set of inputs. These methods relax the original data requirement, but they change the learning problem and should not be interpreted as the same per-scene optimization result. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:42d03ceacbbb] [E:arxiv:2302.10109:abstract:claim:370fdae62ed9]

Memory and hardware compatibility create a separate trade-off when NeRFs are accelerated. Caching or baking a continuous field into sparse voxels can improve rendering speed, but it raises storage or GPU-memory use; SNeRG's precomputed sparse grid, for example, accelerates deferred rendering yet still ray-marches volumetric textures and requires significant GPU memory. MobileNeRF instead moves visibility to textured polygons and z-buffer rasterization so commodity graphics pipelines and mobile GPUs can be used. These are deployment solutions, not free speedups of the original MLP: they alter the representation store and often require baking or a deferred shader. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:72ae3e030d32] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce]

Large scenes intensify both computation and organization costs. A single monolithic ray-marched field does not naturally map to the culling, level-of-detail, and rasterization mechanisms used for urban-scale interactive graphics. Systems such as UE4-NeRF partition scenes and combine optimized mesh-like proxies with game-engine rasterization, while deformable neural mesh primitives seek rasterization efficiency and lower peak memory for urban rendering. Their speed and memory claims depend on those primitives, partitioning, level-of-detail, and engine integration; they do not establish that the unmodified foundational NeRF has the same scalability. [E:arxiv:2310.13263:abstract:claim:d66087edc431] [E:arxiv:2307.10776:abstract:claim:e4c55e718898] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719]

Architecture choice also involves downstream trade-offs beyond average rendering quality. Plain MLPs provide a continuous coordinate field with comparatively clear functional structure, whereas hash tables, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, tri-planes, and hybrid encodings can train or render faster but may have less clear geometric meaning or different memory profiles. PVD's any-to-any distillation and Hyb-NeRF's coarse-to-fine hybrid encoding are responses to this fragmentation: practitioners may convert or combine representations for editing, training speed, rendering speed, or memory. The limitation is that no single store in the selected evidence dominates all of these objectives simultaneously. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:4:97facdcc473c:claim:cec90d41fbf0] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:95df0ad0b144]

The physical scope of the basic emission-absorption model should also be distinguished from full participating-media light transport. The NeRF integral accumulates locally emitted color and density along a camera ray; it does not, in its foundational form, solve multiple scattering or global illumination in a general volumetric medium. Work on volumetric clouds uses a physically based differentiable volume renderer and diffusion prior to provide gradients for multiple-scattering light transport, explicitly contrasting that setting with classic NeRF approaches. Thus, strong scattering media are outside the applicability boundary of the original local radiance-and-density formulation. [E:arxiv:2501.05226:abstract:claim:c3f096e7de3c] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a]

Taken together, these limitations should be attributed to specific parts of the pipeline rather than used as a blanket claim that neural radiance fields are unsuitable. The original formulation's core open trade-offs are: many MLP evaluations per ray, point-sample aliasing under scale change, geometry ambiguity under photometric and view-dependent supervision, per-scene posed-image training, and difficulty matching commodity rasterization hardware without baking or restructuring the field. Later evidence shows that anti-aliasing, feed-forward priors, surface models, reflection tracing, explicit grids, polygons, mesh primitives, and architecture distillation can address individual constraints, but each changes assumptions and introduces its own quality, memory, physical-accuracy, editing, or deployment trade-off. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f]

Conclusion

The core answer is that NeRF combines a 5D neural radiance field with classical differentiable volume rendering: the MLP supplies density and color at queried ray coordinates, transmittance-weighted alpha compositing forms each pixel, and posed-image error supervises the field without explicit 3D labels. The discrete estimator is Ĉ(r)=Σ_i T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i))c_i, with optional remaining-transmittance background weighting. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180]

The main trade-off is expressive, image-based view synthesis against sampling cost: hierarchical sampling concentrates MLP evaluations where coarse weights indicate contribution, but the original method still requires many network queries per ray and is best understood as offline per-scene optimization. Its point-ray formulation also leaves scale aliasing, geometry ambiguity, and deployment acceleration to later modified architectures rather than being solved by the baseline representation itself. fact_fields.method: Elliptical basis function radiance field representation with SH/SG

claim_records.text: RayGauss's ray casting algorithm implementation and backpropagation relies on a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) implemented on GPU with the OptiX library.

claim_records.text: The NeRF method represents a scene using a fully-connected (non-convolutional) deep network that takes a single continuous 5D coordinate (spatial location (x,y,z) and viewing direction (θ, φ)) as input and outputs volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.

fact_fields.method: NeRF scene representation via fully-connected (non-convolutional) deep network

claim_records.text: NeRF synthesizes novel views by querying 5D coordinates along camera rays and using classic volume rendering techniques to project output colors and densities into an image.

fact_fields.method: Classic volume rendering for novel view synthesis

claim_records.text: Because volume rendering is naturally differentiable, the only input required to optimize the NeRF representation is a set of images with known camera poses.

The expected color C(r) of a camera ray r(t) = o + td with near and far bounds tn and tf is computed via the integral C(r) = ∫ from tn to tf of T(t)σ(r(t))c(r(t), d)dt, where T(t) = exp(−∫ from tn to t of σ(r(s))ds).
The volume density σ(x) can be interpreted as the differential probability of a ray terminating at an infinitesimal particle at location x.
The function T(t) denotes the accumulated transmittance along the ray from tn to t, i.e., the probability that the ray travels from tn to t without hitting any other particle.
The NeRF MLP FΘ first processes the input 3D coordinate x with 8 fully-connected layers (using ReLU activations and 256 channels per layer), and outputs σ and a 256-dimensional feature vector.

fact_fields.method: NeRF MLP architecture for processing 3D coordinates

claim_records.text: The 256-dimensional feature vector output by the initial 8 layers is concatenated with the camera ray's viewing direction and passed to one additional fully-connected layer (using a ReLU activation and 128 channels) that outputs the view-dependent RGB color.
