claims: The NeRF method represents a scene using a fully-connected (non-convolutional) deep network that takes a single continuous 5D coordinate (spatial location (x,y,z) and viewing direction (θ, φ)) as input and outputs volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.
NeRF synthesizes novel views by querying 5D coordinates along camera rays and using classic volume rendering techniques to project output colors and densities into an image.
Because volume rendering is naturally differentiable, the only input required to optimize the NeRF representation is a set of images with known camera poses.

The expected color C(r) of a camera ray r(t) = o + td with near and far bounds tn and tf is computed via the integral C(r) = ∫ from tn to tf of T(t)σ(r(t))c(r(t), d)dt, where T(t) = exp(−∫ from tn to t of σ(r(s))ds).
The volume density σ(x) can be interpreted as the differential probability of a ray terminating at an infinitesimal particle at location x.
The function T(t) denotes the accumulated transmittance along the ray from tn to t, i.e., the probability that the ray travels from tn to t without hitting any other particle.
The NeRF MLP FΘ first processes the input 3D coordinate x with 8 fully-connected layers (using ReLU activations and 256 channels per layer), and outputs σ and a 256-dimensional feature vector.

The 256-dimensional feature vector output by the initial 8 layers is concatenated with the camera ray's viewing direction and passed to one additional fully-connected layer (using a ReLU activation and 128 channels) that outputs the view-dependent RGB color.

The NeRF representation encourages multiview consistency by restricting the network to predict volume density σ as a function of only location x, while allowing RGB color c to be predicted as a function of both location and viewing direction.

The hierarchical volume sampling procedure simultaneously optimizes two networks: one "coarse" and one "fine", to increase rendering efficiency by allocating samples proportionally to their expected effect on the final rendering.
In hierarchical volume sampling, a set of Nc locations is first sampled using stratified sampling, and the "coarse" network is evaluated at these locations.
The alpha composited color from the coarse network Ĉc(r) is rewritten as a weighted sum of all sampled colors ci along the ray: Ĉc(r) = Σ from i=1 to Nc of wi ci, where wi = Ti(1 − exp(−σiδi)).
Normalizing the coarse network weights as ŵi = wi / Σ from j=1 to Nc of wj produces a piecewise-constant PDF along the ray.

A second set of Nf locations is sampled from the piecewise-constant PDF using inverse transform sampling, the "fine" network is evaluated at the union of the first and second set of samples, and the final rendered color of the ray Ĉf(r) is computed using all Nc+Nf samples.

Two improvements are introduced to enable NeRF to represent high-resolution complex scenes: a positional encoding of input coordinates that assists the MLP in representing high-frequency functions, and a hierarchical sampling procedure that allows efficient sampling of this high-frequency representation.
Having the network FΘ directly operate on xyzθφ input coordinates results in renderings that perform poorly at representing high-frequency variation in color and geometry.

The positional encoding function γ(p) = (sin(2^0 πp), cos(2^0 πp), ..., sin(2^{L-1} πp), cos(2^{L-1} πp)) is applied separately to each of the three coordinate values in x (normalized to lie in [−1, 1]) and to the three components of the Cartesian viewing direction unit vector d (which lie in [−1, 1]).
In NeRF experiments, L = 10 is used for the positional encoding of spatial coordinates γ(x) and L = 4 is used for the positional encoding of viewing directions γ(d).

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) rely upon specialized volumetric rendering algorithms based on ray marching that are mismatched to the capabilities of widely deployed graphics hardware.
MobileNeRF represents a NeRF as a set of polygons with textures representing binary opacities and feature vectors.

Traditional rendering of MobileNeRF polygons with a z-buffer yields an image with features at every pixel, which are interpreted by a small, view-dependent MLP running in a fragment shader to produce a final pixel color.

MobileNeRF enables NeRFs to be rendered with the traditional polygon rasterization pipeline, which provides massive pixel-level parallelism, achieving interactive frame rates on a wide range of compute platforms, including mobile phones.

Traditional NeRF implementations use a volumetric rendering algorithm that evaluates a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions along the ray for each pixel in order to estimate and integrate density and radiance.
The traditional NeRF volumetric rendering process is far too slow for interactive visualization.
SNeRG (Sparse Neural Radiance Grids) precomputation and deferred rendering approach increases the rendering speed of NeRF by three orders of magnitude.

SNeRG still relies upon ray marching through a sparse voxel grid to produce the features for each pixel, and thus it cannot fully utilize the parallelism available in commodity graphics processing units (GPUs).
SNeRG requires a significant amount of GPU memory to store the volumetric textures, which prohibits it from running on common mobile devices.
MobileNeRF's rendering pipeline does not sample rays or sort polygons in depth order, and thus can model only binary opacities.
MobileNeRF is 10× faster than SNeRG with the same output quality on standard test scenes.

fact_fields.method: MobileNeRF vs SNeRG rendering speed comparison

claim_records.text: MobileNeRF consumes less memory by storing surface textures instead of volumetric textures, enabling the method to run on integrated GPUs with limited memory and power.
MobileNeRF runs on a web browser and is compatible with all devices tested, as its viewer is an HTML webpage.
MobileNeRF allows real-time manipulation of reconstructed objects/scenes, as they are simple triangle meshes.
MobileNeRF does not need reconstructed 3D geometry as input.
Point-based representations for view synthesis often result in a lack of 3D consistency because their convolutional post-processing runs independently per output frame.
Point-based view synthesis representations require powerful desktop GPUs and have not been demonstrated to run on a mobile device.
DefTet differentiably renders a tetrahedral grid with occupancy and color at each vertex, then composites the interpolated values at all intersected faces along a ray.
NVDiffRec combines differentiable marching tetrahedra with differentiable rasterization to perform full inverse rendering and extract triangle meshes, materials, and lighting from images.
Differentiable inverse-rendering representations like DefTet and NVDiffRec incur a significant loss in view-synthesis quality.
While real-time rendering is possible with simple lighting for differentiable inverse-rendering representations, global illumination (GI) is computationally infeasible on mobile hardware.
MobileNeRF simply caches the outgoing radiance, which does not need expensive compute to model GI effects, and also results in higher view-synthesis quality.
Rendering a NeRF involves evaluating a large neural network at multiple 3D locations per pixel, preventing real-time rendering.

claim_records.text: Progressive Volume Distillation (PVD) is a systematic distillation method that enables any-to-any conversions between different NeRF architectures, including MLP, sparse or low-rank tensors, hashtables and their compositions.

PVD performs distillation progressively on different levels of volume representations from shallower to deeper, and employs special treatment of density to address its specific numerical instability problem.

With PVD, an MLP-based NeRF model distilled from a hashtable-based Instant-NGP model achieves a 10×~20× faster speed than training the original NeRF from scratch, while achieving a superior level of synthesis quality.
PVD is validated empirically on the NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF and TanksAndTemples datasets.
Hashtable-based NeRF representations admit faster training and rendering, but their lack of clear geometric meaning hampers downstream tasks like spatial-relation-aware editing.

In the Family and Barn scenes from the TanksAndTemples dataset, a NeRF model distilled by PVD from an INGP teacher within 1.5 hours achieves improved synthesis quality compared to a NeRF model trained from scratch using 25 hours.
PVD uses loss on intermediate volume representations (including output of φ1*, color and density) alongside the final rendered RGB volume to accelerate distillation.
PVD employs a special treatment of the dynamic density volume range by clipping, which improves training stability and significantly improves synthesis quality.
Distillation from hashtable and VM-decomposition structures often helps boost student model synthesis quality and consumes less time than training from scratch.
PVD builds a block-wise distillation strategy to accelerate the training procedure based on a unified view of different NeRF architectures.

NeRF architectures including plain MLP, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, hashtables and their compositions each have particular sets of trade-offs between training speed, rendering speed, and downstream task suitability.
PVD empowers downstream applications to optimally adapt neural NeRF representations for the task at hand in a post hoc fashion.

claim_records.text: NeRF generates a volumetric representation called a radiance field that creates color and density for every point within the relevant 3D space, rather than directly restoring the whole 3D scene geometry.
NeRF uses an interpolation approach to produce new 3D reconstructed views of complicated scenes.
CAMPARI simultaneously learns a camera generator and an image generator, enabling use of complex camera distributions without manual tuning.
CAMPARI represents scenes through foreground and background decomposition, leading to 3D-consistent representations and accurate camera distribution recovery.
CAMPARI surpasses baseline models that heavily depend on accurately matched camera distributions, due to its performance without camera parameter tuning.
Pix2NeRF introduces a pipeline to generate NeRF from a single input image, built upon π-GAN which maps latent codes to radiance fields.
Pix2NeRF employs an unsupervised approach and can be trained with independent images, with potential applications in 3D avatar generation, novel view synthesis, and super-resolution.
Pix2NeRF is currently restricted to work with only one category per dataset, impeding its ability to generalize to new categories.
Pix2NeRF is built on top of π-GAN but is not limited to using π-GAN as its backbone; newer generative NeRF models such as EG3D may achieve better visual quality if used as a backbone.

NeRF uses a deep neural network to represent complex scenes in a fully connected, non-convolutional way, with input as a continuous 5D coordinate and output as volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.
The 5D coordinate space for NeRF includes three dimensions for spatial coordinates (x,y,z) and two dimensions for camera viewing angles (θ,φ).
NeRF uses classic volume rendering techniques to synthesize views and is optimized using a set of images with known camera poses.
NeRF introduces a positional encoding and a hierarchical sampling strategy to address the inefficiency of the basic implementation.
Using input viewing direction, NeRF can represent non-Lambertian effects such as specularities.
NeRF uses a separate neural continuous volume representation network for each scene.
This survey categorizes and compares recent NeRF advances according to their architectural designs, especially in the field of novel view synthesis.

claim_records.text: The introduced single-view volumetric reconstruction technique models unknown volumetric field distributions using an unconditional diffusion model trained on a novel benchmark dataset of 1,000 synthetically simulated volumetric density fields.

fact_fields.method: unconditional diffusion model for single-view volumetric reconstruction

claim_records.text: The neural diffusion model is trained on latent codes of a novel diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation.

A physically-based differentiable volume renderer is employed to provide gradients with respect to light transport in latent space, making reconstructions better aligned with observed data compared to classic NeRF approaches.
The diffusion model is trained on a dataset of 1,000 synthetically simulated volumetric density fields specifically consisting of cumulus clouds for the case study.

The proposed approach couples the renderer with the diffusion model to reconstruct radiance parameters using the prior for density distribution but not for appearance, so the 3D density field can be trained solely on the prior without requiring images of all possible backgrounds and light scattering effects.

fact_fields.method: diffusion prior guided physically-based differentiable volume renderer reconstruction

claim_records.text: The key contributions include a large database of 3D cumulus cloud-like density fields generated using numerical fluid simulation.
The key contributions include a 3D cloud decoder utilizing a novel diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation, trained jointly on a subset of the database.

fact_fields.method: 3D cloud decoder with diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation

claim_records.text: The key contributions include a novel Parametric Diffusion Posterior Sampling (PDPS) technique utilizing a shape-centric prior with a physically-based differentiable volume renderer.
To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first approach that integrates an unconditional diffusion model trained on volumetric density distributions with a differentiable volume renderer.

fact_fields.method: integrated unconditional diffusion model and differentiable volume renderer

claim_records.text: The proposed approach demonstrates potential across tasks including single- and multi-view reconstruction, and volume super-resolution.

fact_fields.method: light transport-aware diffusion posterior sampling for volumetric reconstruction

claim_records.text: Reconstructing the internal density distribution of highly dense volumes is widely considered nearly impossible due to high uncertainty in the light scattering process and presence of vanishing gradients, a limitation that can only be alleviated by incorporating prior information during reconstruction.

For complex volumetric materials such as clouds, smoke, or fire, the reconstruction problem becomes so ill-posed that it requires dozens, if not hundreds, of different views to adequately constrain object parameters.

claim_records.text: Hyb-NeRF is a neural radiance field with a multi-resolution hybrid encoding that uses memory-efficient learnable positional features at coarse resolutions and hash-based feature grids at fine resolutions, achieving efficient neural modeling, fast rendering, and high-quality novel view synthesis.
Cone tracing-based features are embedded in the learnable positional encoding of Hyb-NeRF to eliminate encoding ambiguity and reduce aliasing artifacts.

fact_fields.method: cone tracing-based feature embedding in learnable positional encoding

claim_records.text: Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show Hyb-NeRF achieves faster rendering speed, better rendering quality, and lower memory footprint compared to previous state-of-the-art methods.
On the ficus scene in Blender, Hyb-NeRF with 16.4M parameters achieves 35.85 PSNR and 0.986 SSIM, compared to JNGP with 24.4M parameters achieving 33.23 PSNR and 0.981 SSIM.
All Hyb-NeRF models can reconstruct high-quality radiance fields in 9 minutes.

The smallest Hyb-NeRF model with 8.4M trainable parameters takes 4 minutes to achieve better rendering quality than state-of-the-art methods while requiring substantially less memory than previous and concurrent voxel-based methods.

Hyb-NeRF concatenates coarse-level learnable positional features with fine-level multi-resolution feature grids for multi-resolution scene representation, yielding detailed 3D reconstructions and high-quality rendering.
NeRF requires hundreds of network evaluations per pixel to approximate a volume rendering integral, making it slow to train.
Caching NeRFs into explicit data structures can effectively enhance rendering speed but at the cost of higher memory usage.

fact_fields.method: explicit data structure caching for NeRF

claim_records.text: Hash-based multi-resolution grid representation is fast to train and well suited to fast operation, but trainable features at coarse resolution levels have lower resolutions and are less compressed than feature grids at fine resolution levels, resulting in limited representation power and low memory efficiency.

claim_records.text: NeRF's rendering procedure samples a scene with a single ray per pixel and may produce renderings that are excessively blurred or aliased when training or testing images observe scene content at different resolutions.

The straightforward solution of supersampling by rendering with multiple rays per pixel is impractical for NeRF, because rendering each ray requires querying a multilayer perceptron hundreds of times.

fact_fields.method: supersampling with multiple rays per pixel

claim_records.text: mip-NeRF extends NeRF to represent the scene at a continuously-valued scale by efficiently rendering anti-aliased conical frustums instead of rays.
mip-NeRF reduces objectionable aliasing artifacts and significantly improves NeRF's ability to represent fine details, while also being 7% faster than NeRF and half the size.
Compared to NeRF, mip-NeRF reduces average error rates by 17% on the dataset presented with NeRF.
Compared to NeRF, mip-NeRF reduces average error rates by 60% on a challenging multiscale variant of the NeRF dataset.
Mip-NeRF is able to match the accuracy of a brute-force supersampled NeRF on the multiscale dataset while being 22x faster.

Mip-NeRF reasons about the 3D conical frustum defined by a camera pixel, and featurizes these conical frustums with integrated positional encoding (IPE) by approximating the frustum with a multivariate Gaussian and computing the closed-form integral E[γ(x)] over positional encodings of coordinates within the Gaussian.
When training images observe scene content at multiple resolutions, renderings from the recovered NeRF appear excessively blurred in close-up views and contain aliasing artifacts in distant views.

Mip-NeRF's scale-aware structure allows merging the separate 'coarse' and 'fine' MLPs used by NeRF for hierarchical sampling into a single MLP, making mip-NeRF slightly faster than NeRF (~7%) and having half as many parameters.
A NeRF trained on full-resolution images produces photorealistic renderings at new view locations only at the resolution or scale of the training images.
Adjusting camera intrinsics to reduce image resolution for a NeRF trained on full-resolution images results in renderings that exhibit severe aliasing.
Training a NeRF on multi-resolution images ameliorates aliasing issues slightly but results in poor quality renderings across scales: blur at full resolution, and 'jaggies' at low resolutions.
Mip-NeRF trained on multi-resolution images is capable of producing photorealistic renderings across different scales.

claim_records.text: An augmentation of the training data is proposed that relaxes the periodicity assumption of the Fourier compression used in Fourier PlenOctrees.
PlenOctrees use a hierarchical octree structure of density and view-dependent radiance in terms of spherical harmonics (SH) to entirely avoid network evaluations.
Instant-NGP incorporated a multi-resolution hash encoding to significantly accelerate the training of neural models including NeRF.
Plenoxels stored SH and opacity values within a sparse voxel grid.
TensoRF factorized dense voxel grids into multiple low-rank components.

Fourier PlenOctrees (FPO) relaxed the limitation of ordinary PlenOctrees to only capture static scenes in a hierarchical manner by combining it with the Fourier transform which enables handling time-variant density and SH-based radiance in an efficient way.
During FPO construction, compression is performed on encoded densities σ′ = ecomp(elog(σ)), where the encoding consists of a component-dependent part and a logarithmic part.
The proposed encoding allows for a better reconstruction of the original densities without any fine-tuning than can be achieved with only the DFT and IDFT as proposed for FPOs.

fact_fields.method: proposed component-dependent + logarithmic density encoding vs DFT/IDFT-only FPO

claim_records.text: Non-negative density values σ are encoded logarithmically using elog(σ) = log(σ + 1) before applying the DFT, with the shift by 1 chosen so that elog remains a non-negative function for non-negative input densities with elog(0) = 0.
The logarithmic density encoding maps larger density values closer together while keeping smaller values almost unchanged, focusing approximation on densities near or equal to zero.
The encoded density sequences are easier to approximate with a low-frequency Fourier basis exploiting the properties of the transfer function.
The L2-error in fine-tuning is allowed to be larger for encoded high density values than without logarithmic encoding, focusing optimization on the more important parts of the reconstruction.
During rendering, the inverse of the logarithmic encoding elog(σ) = log(σ + 1) is applied after the IDFT to project densities back to their original range.

claim_records.text: Existing 3D reconstruction methods including NeRF require excessive runtime for rendering, making them impractical for daily applications.
EvaSurf first employs an efficient surface-based model with a multi-view supervision module to ensure accurate mesh reconstruction.
EvaSurf learns an implicit texture embedded with a set of Gaussian lobes to capture view-dependent information for high-fidelity rendering.
EvaSurf employs a lightweight neural shader with explicit geometry and implicit texture to reduce computation expense and support real-time rendering on common mobile devices.

EvaSurf can run on mobile devices at over 40 FPS (Frames Per Second).
The final package required for EvaSurf rendering takes up only 40-50 MB.

claim_records.text: The rendering scheme in neural radiance field (NeRF) is effective in rendering a pixel by casting a ray into the scene.
NeRF yields blurred rendering results when the training images are captured at non-uniform scales.
NeRF produces aliasing artifacts if the test images are taken in distant views.
Mip-NeRF proposes a multiscale representation as a conical frustum to encode scale information.
Mip-NeRF is only suitable for offline rendering since it relies on integrated positional encoding (IPE) to query a multilayer perceptron (MLP).
Mip-VoG is an explicit multiscale representation with a deferred architecture for real-time anti-aliasing rendering.
Mip-VoG includes a density Mip-VoG for scene geometry and a feature Mip-VoG with a small MLP for view-dependent color.
Mip-VoG encodes scene scale using the level of detail (LOD) derived from ray differentials.
Mip-VoG uses quadrilinear interpolation to map a queried 3D location to its features and density from two neighboring downsampled voxel grids.
Mip-VoG is the first approach to offer multiscale training and real-time anti-aliasing rendering simultaneously.
Experiments on multiscale datasets show that Mip-VoG outperforms state-of-the-art real-time rendering baselines.

claim_records.text: CLIP-NeRF is a multi-modal 3D object manipulation method for neural radiance fields that leverages the joint language-image embedding space of the CLIP model.
CLIP-NeRF allows manipulating NeRF using either a short text prompt or an exemplar image.
CLIP-NeRF introduces a disentangled conditional NeRF architecture that allows individual control over both shape and appearance.
In CLIP-NeRF, shape conditioning is achieved by applying a learned deformation field to the positional encoding, and color conditioning is deferred to the volumetric rendering stage.
CLIP-NeRF designs two code mappers that take a CLIP embedding as input and update the latent codes to reflect the targeted editing.
The CLIP-NeRF code mappers are trained with a CLIP-based matching loss to ensure manipulation accuracy.
CLIP-NeRF proposes an inverse optimization method that accurately projects an input image to the latent codes for manipulation to enable editing on real images.
CLIP-NeRF is evaluated via extensive experiments on a variety of text prompts and exemplar images, and provides an intuitive interface for interactive editing.

claim_records.text: NeRF trains a deep network to map 5D input coordinates representing spatial location and viewing direction into a volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance.
NeRF is only applicable to static scenes where the same spatial location can be queried from different images.

D-NeRF extends neural radiance fields to a dynamic domain, allowing reconstruction and rendering of novel images of objects under rigid and non-rigid motions from a single camera moving around the scene.

D-NeRF treats time as an additional input and splits learning into two stages: one encoding the scene into a canonical space, and another mapping the canonical representation into the deformed scene at a particular time.
Both mappings in D-NeRF are simultaneously learned using fully-connected networks.
After training, D-NeRF can render novel images while controlling both the camera view and the time variable, and thus the object movement.
D-NeRF demonstrates effectiveness on scenes with objects under rigid, articulated and non-rigid motions.

claim_records.text: NeRF has emerged as a powerful representation for novel view synthesis due to its simplicity and state-of-the-art performance.
NeRF can produce photorealistic renderings of unseen viewpoints when many input views are available.
NeRF performance drops significantly when the number of input views is reduced.
The majority of artifacts in sparse input NeRF scenarios are caused by errors in estimated scene geometry and by divergent behavior at the start of training.
RegNeRF regularizes the geometry and appearance of patches rendered from unobserved viewpoints, and anneals the ray sampling space during training.
RegNeRF additionally uses a normalizing flow model to regularize the color of unobserved viewpoints.
RegNeRF outperforms other methods that optimize over a single scene.
In many cases, RegNeRF also outperforms conditional models that are extensively pre-trained on large multi-view datasets.

claim_records.text: NeRF and its variants require a lengthy training time ranging from hours to days for reconstructing a single scene.
The proposed direct voxel grid optimization approach achieves NeRF-comparable quality and converges from scratch in less than 15 minutes with a single GPU.
The proposed representation uses a density voxel grid for scene geometry and a feature voxel grid with a shallow network for complex view-dependent appearance.
Post-activation interpolation on voxel density is capable of producing sharp surfaces in lower grid resolution.
Imposing several priors robustifies the direct voxel density optimization process, which is otherwise prone to suboptimal geometry solutions.

fact_fields.method: Imposing several priors on direct voxel density optimization

claim_records.text: Evaluation on five inward-facing benchmarks shows the proposed method matches, if not surpasses, NeRF's quality while taking about 15 minutes to train from scratch for a new scene.

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) have low rendering efficiency due to the need for multiple network forwardings to render a single pixel.
Existing Neural Light Field (NeLF) methods require significantly larger network capacities to achieve visual quality close to NeRF, which limits their rendering efficiency in practice.
The proposed Neural Radiance Distribution Field (NeRDF) uses a small network similar to NeRF while preserving rendering speed with a single network forwarding per pixel as in NeLF.
The proposed NeRDF method achieves a ~254x speed-up over NeRF with similar network size, with only a marginal performance decline.
The proposed NeRDF method offers a better trade-off among speed, quality, and network size than existing methods.

claim_records.text: The introduced 3D Hierarchical Proxy Node representation represents an object's shape and texture via a sparse set of hierarchically organized (tree-structured) proxy nodes distributed on its surface and interior, with each node storing local shape and texture information implicitly encoded by a small MLP within its neighborhood.
Querying any 3D coordinate's properties in the Hierarchical Proxy Node framework involves efficient neural interpolation and lightweight decoding from relevant nearby and parent nodes.

The Hierarchical Proxy Node framework yields a highly compact representation where nodes align with local semantics, enabling direct drag-and-edit manipulation and offering scalable quality-complexity control.
Extensive experiments across 3D reconstruction and editing demonstrate the HPR3D method's expressive efficiency, high-fidelity rendering quality, and superior editability.

Current 3D representations including meshes, voxels, point clouds, and NeRF-based neural implicit fields are often task-specific, lacking universal applicability across reconstruction, generation, editing, and driving.
NeRFs deliver excellent rendering but suffer from structural ambiguity, hindering animation and manipulation.
Meshes offer high precision but their dense vertex data complicates editing.

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) typically struggle to reconstruct and render highly specular objects, whose appearance varies quickly with changes in viewpoint.
Recent NeRF works have improved ability to render detailed specular appearance of distant environment illumination, but are unable to synthesize consistent reflections of closer content.

fact_fields.method: recent NeRF-based specular appearance modeling approaches

claim_records.text: These recent specular NeRF techniques rely on large computationally-expensive neural networks to model outgoing radiance, which severely limits optimization and rendering speed.

The proposed NeRF-Casting approach casts reflection rays from points along each camera ray and traces them through the NeRF representation to render feature vectors which are decoded into color using a small inexpensive network, instead of querying an expensive neural network for outgoing view-dependent radiance at those points.
The NeRF-Casting model outperforms prior methods for view synthesis of scenes containing shiny objects.
NeRF-Casting is the only existing NeRF method that can synthesize photorealistic specular appearance and reflections in real-world scenes.
NeRF-Casting requires comparable optimization time to current state-of-the-art view synthesis models.

claim_records.text: Rendering a single pixel in NeRF requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times.
Rendering a pixel in NeLF amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching.
The proposed method uses a deep residual MLP network with 88 layers to effectively learn the light field.
The key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which knowledge is transferred from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation.
On synthetic scenes, the proposed method achieves 26-35x FLOPs reduction per camera ray compared to NeRF.
On synthetic scenes, the proposed method achieves 28-31x runtime speedup compared to NeRF.
On synthetic scenes, the proposed method delivers 1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement over NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

claim_records.text: Existing Human NeRF methods for reconstructing 3D humans typically rely on multiple 2D images from multi-view cameras or monocular videos captured from fixed camera views.

SHERF uses a feature fusion transformer to effectively integrate the 3D-aware hierarchical feature bank.

Extensive experiments on THuman, RenderPeople, ZJU_MoCap, and HuMMan datasets demonstrate that SHERF achieves state-of-the-art performance, with better generalizability for novel view and pose synthesis.

claim_records.text: The presented method synthesizes novel views of complex scenes by interpolating a sparse set of nearby views.

The core network architecture of the method includes a multilayer perceptron and a ray transformer that estimates radiance and volume density at continuous 5D locations (3D spatial locations and 2D viewing directions).
The method draws appearance information on the fly from multiple source views at render time.
Drawing on source views at render time allows the method to render high-resolution imagery.
Unlike neural scene representation work that optimizes per-scene functions for rendering, the method learns a generic view interpolation function that generalizes to novel scenes.
The method renders images using classic volume rendering, which is fully differentiable and allows training using only multi-view posed images as supervision.
Experiments show that the method outperforms recent novel view synthesis methods that also seek to generalize to novel scenes.
If fine-tuned on each scene, the method is competitive with state-of-the-art single-scene neural rendering methods.

claim_records.text: 3DGS is introduced into indoor 3D Object Detection for the first time in this work.
3DGS primarily relies on 2D pixel-level supervision, resulting in unclear 3D spatial distribution of Gaussian blobs and poor differentiation between objects and background, which hinders indoor 3DOD.
2D images typically include numerous background pixels, leading to densely reconstructed 3DGS with many noisy Gaussian blobs representing the background, negatively affecting detection.
Incorporating 2D Boundary Guidance significantly enhances the spatial distribution of Gaussian blobs, resulting in clearer differentiation between objects and their background.

The proposed Box-Focused Sampling strategy uses 2D boxes to generate object probability distribution in 3D space, allowing effective probabilistic sampling in 3D to retain more object blobs and reduce noisy background blobs.
3DGS-DET achieves an improvement of +6.0 on mAP@0.25 over NeRF-Det++ on the ScanNet dataset.
3DGS-DET achieves an improvement of +7.8 on mAP@0.5 over NeRF-Det++ on the ScanNet dataset.
3DGS-DET achieves an improvement of +14.9 on mAP@0.25 over NeRF-Det++ on the ARKITScenes dataset.
NeRF has been adapted for indoor 3D Object Detection via view-synthesis representation, but its implicit nature limits representational capacity.

claim_records.text: VDN-NeRF is a method to train neural radiance fields for better geometry under non-Lambertian surface and dynamic lighting conditions that cause significant variation in the radiance of a point when viewed from different angles.

VDN-NeRF normalizes view-dependence by distilling invariant information already encoded in the learned NeRFs, rather than explicitly modeling the underlying factors that result in the view-dependent phenomenon.
VDN-NeRF jointly trains NeRFs for view synthesis with view-dependence normalization to attain quality geometry.

Experiments show that even though shape-radiance ambiguity is inevitable, the proposed normalization can minimize its effect on geometry, which essentially aligns the optimal capacity needed for explaining view-dependent variations.
VDN-NeRF applies to various baselines and significantly improves geometry without changing the volume rendering pipeline, even if the data is captured under a moving light source.

claim_records.text: Neural approaches such as NeRF have achieved remarkable success in view synthesis, but do not explicitly perform decomposition and instead operate exclusively on radiance, the product of reflectance and illumination.
Extensions to NeRF, such as NeRD, can perform decomposition but struggle to accurately recover detailed illumination, thereby significantly limiting realism.
The proposed reflectance decomposition network can estimate shape, BRDF, and per-image illumination given a set of object images captured under varying illumination.
Neural-PIL is a novel illumination integration network that replaces a costly illumination integral operation in the rendering with a simple network query.
Deep low-dimensional priors on BRDF and illumination representations are learned using novel smooth manifold auto-encoders.
The decompositions can result in considerably better BRDF and light estimates enabling more accurate novel view-synthesis and relighting compared to prior art.

claim_records.text: NeuDA is a flexible neural implicit representation leveraging hierarchical voxel grids for high-fidelity surface reconstruction.
Each vertex in NeuDA's hierarchical anchor grids stores a 3D position (anchor) instead of a direct embedding (feature).
Optimizing NeuDA's anchor grids allows different local geometry structures to be adaptively encoded.
NeuDA introduces a simple hierarchical positional encoding method for the hierarchical anchor structure to flexibly exploit properties of high-frequency and low-frequency geometry and appearance.
Experiments on both the DTU and BlendedMVS datasets demonstrate that NeuDA can produce promising mesh surfaces.

Previous differentiable ray casting works IDR and NeuS overlook spatial context in 3D space when predicting and rendering surfaces, and may fail to capture sharp local topologies such as small holes and structures.

claim_records.text: Prior radiance field methods achieving high visual quality require neural networks that are costly to train and render.
Recent faster radiance field methods inevitably trade off speed for quality.
For unbounded and complete scenes rather than isolated objects at 1080p resolution rendering, no current method can achieve real-time display rates.
The introduced 3D Gaussian splatting method achieves state-of-the-art visual quality while maintaining competitive training times and high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis at 1080p resolution.
The introduced method represents scenes with 3D Gaussians starting from sparse points produced during camera calibration.
The introduced method performs interleaved optimization and density control of 3D Gaussians, notably optimizing anisotropic covariance to achieve an accurate representation of the scene.
The introduced method develops a fast visibility-aware rendering algorithm that supports anisotropic splatting and both accelerates training and allows real-time rendering.
The introduced method achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and real-time rendering on several established datasets.

claim_records.text: The NeRF method represents a scene using a fully-connected (non-convolutional) deep network that takes a single continuous 5D coordinate (spatial location (x,y,z) and viewing direction (θ, φ)) as input and outputs volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.

fact_fields.method: NeRF scene representation via fully-connected (non-convolutional) deep network

claim_records.text: NeRF synthesizes novel views by querying 5D coordinates along camera rays and using classic volume rendering techniques to project output colors and densities into an image.

fact_fields.method: Classic volume rendering for novel view synthesis

claim_records.text: Because volume rendering is naturally differentiable, the only input required to optimize the NeRF representation is a set of images with known camera poses.

The expected color C(r) of a camera ray r(t) = o + td with near and far bounds tn and tf is computed via the integral C(r) = ∫ from tn to tf of T(t)σ(r(t))c(r(t), d)dt, where T(t) = exp(−∫ from tn to t of σ(r(s))ds).
The volume density σ(x) can be interpreted as the differential probability of a ray terminating at an infinitesimal particle at location x.
The function T(t) denotes the accumulated transmittance along the ray from tn to t, i.e., the probability that the ray travels from tn to t without hitting any other particle.
The NeRF MLP FΘ first processes the input 3D coordinate x with 8 fully-connected layers (using ReLU activations and 256 channels per layer), and outputs σ and a 256-dimensional feature vector.

fact_fields.method: NeRF MLP architecture for processing 3D coordinates

claim_records.text: The 256-dimensional feature vector output by the initial 8 layers is concatenated with the camera ray's viewing direction and passed to one additional fully-connected layer (using a ReLU activation and 128 channels) that outputs the view-dependent RGB color.

fact_fields.method: NeRF MLP architecture for processing viewing direction

claim_records.text: The NeRF representation encourages multiview consistency by restricting the network to predict volume density σ as a function of only location x, while allowing RGB color c to be predicted as a function of both location and viewing direction.

The hierarchical volume sampling procedure simultaneously optimizes two networks: one "coarse" and one "fine", to increase rendering efficiency by allocating samples proportionally to their expected effect on the final rendering.

fact_fields.method: Hierarchical volume sampling with coarse and fine networks

claim_records.text: In hierarchical volume sampling, a set of Nc locations is first sampled using stratified sampling, and the "coarse" network is evaluated at these locations.

fact_fields.method: Stratified sampling for coarse network evaluation

claim_records.text: The alpha composited color from the coarse network Ĉc(r) is rewritten as a weighted sum of all sampled colors ci along the ray: Ĉc(r) = Σ from i=1 to Nc of wi ci, where wi = Ti(1 − exp(−σiδi)).

fact_fields.method: Weighted sum formulation for coarse network rendered color

claim_records.text: Normalizing the coarse network weights as ŵi = wi / Σ from j=1 to Nc of wj produces a piecewise-constant PDF along the ray.

fact_fields.method: Normalization of coarse network weights to form PDF

claim_records.text: A second set of Nf locations is sampled from the piecewise-constant PDF using inverse transform sampling, the "fine" network is evaluated at the union of the first and second set of samples, and the final rendered color of the ray Ĉf(r) is computed using all Nc+Nf samples.

fact_fields.method: Inverse transform sampling for fine network evaluation

claim_records.text: Two improvements are introduced to enable NeRF to represent high-resolution complex scenes: a positional encoding of input coordinates that assists the MLP in representing high-frequency functions, and a hierarchical sampling procedure that allows efficient sampling of this high-frequency representation.

fact_fields.method: NeRF optimization improvements for high-resolution scenes

claim_records.text: Having the network FΘ directly operate on xyzθφ input coordinates results in renderings that perform poorly at representing high-frequency variation in color and geometry.

fact_fields.method: Direct MLP operation on raw input coordinates

claim_records.text: The positional encoding function γ(p) = (sin(2^0 πp), cos(2^0 πp), ..., sin(2^{L-1} πp), cos(2^{L-1} πp)) is applied separately to each of the three coordinate values in x (normalized to lie in [−1, 1]) and to the three components of the Cartesian viewing direction unit vector d (which lie in [−1, 1]).

fact_fields.method: Positional encoding application to input coordinates

claim_records.text: In NeRF experiments, L = 10 is used for the positional encoding of spatial coordinates γ(x) and L = 4 is used for the positional encoding of viewing directions γ(d).

claims: The NeRF method represents a scene using a fully-connected (non-convolutional) deep network that takes a single continuous 5D coordinate (spatial location (x,y,z) and viewing direction (θ, φ)) as input and outputs volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.
NeRF synthesizes novel views by querying 5D coordinates along camera rays and using classic volume rendering techniques to project output colors and densities into an image.
Because volume rendering is naturally differentiable, the only input required to optimize the NeRF representation is a set of images with known camera poses.

The expected color C(r) of a camera ray r(t) = o + td with near and far bounds tn and tf is computed via the integral C(r) = ∫ from tn to tf of T(t)σ(r(t))c(r(t), d)dt, where T(t) = exp(−∫ from tn to t of σ(r(s))ds).
The volume density σ(x) can be interpreted as the differential probability of a ray terminating at an infinitesimal particle at location x.
The function T(t) denotes the accumulated transmittance along the ray from tn to t, i.e., the probability that the ray travels from tn to t without hitting any other particle.
The NeRF MLP FΘ first processes the input 3D coordinate x with 8 fully-connected layers (using ReLU activations and 256 channels per layer), and outputs σ and a 256-dimensional feature vector.

The 256-dimensional feature vector output by the initial 8 layers is concatenated with the camera ray's viewing direction and passed to one additional fully-connected layer (using a ReLU activation and 128 channels) that outputs the view-dependent RGB color.

The NeRF representation encourages multiview consistency by restricting the network to predict volume density σ as a function of only location x, while allowing RGB color c to be predicted as a function of both location and viewing direction.

The hierarchical volume sampling procedure simultaneously optimizes two networks: one "coarse" and one "fine", to increase rendering efficiency by allocating samples proportionally to their expected effect on the final rendering.
In hierarchical volume sampling, a set of Nc locations is first sampled using stratified sampling, and the "coarse" network is evaluated at these locations.
The alpha composited color from the coarse network Ĉc(r) is rewritten as a weighted sum of all sampled colors ci along the ray: Ĉc(r) = Σ from i=1 to Nc of wi ci, where wi = Ti(1 − exp(−σiδi)).
Normalizing the coarse network weights as ŵi = wi / Σ from j=1 to Nc of wj produces a piecewise-constant PDF along the ray.

A second set of Nf locations is sampled from the piecewise-constant PDF using inverse transform sampling, the "fine" network is evaluated at the union of the first and second set of samples, and the final rendered color of the ray Ĉf(r) is computed using all Nc+Nf samples.

Two improvements are introduced to enable NeRF to represent high-resolution complex scenes: a positional encoding of input coordinates that assists the MLP in representing high-frequency functions, and a hierarchical sampling procedure that allows efficient sampling of this high-frequency representation.
Having the network FΘ directly operate on xyzθφ input coordinates results in renderings that perform poorly at representing high-frequency variation in color and geometry.

The positional encoding function γ(p) = (sin(2^0 πp), cos(2^0 πp), ..., sin(2^{L-1} πp), cos(2^{L-1} πp)) is applied separately to each of the three coordinate values in x (normalized to lie in [−1, 1]) and to the three components of the Cartesian viewing direction unit vector d (which lie in [−1, 1]).
In NeRF experiments, L = 10 is used for the positional encoding of spatial coordinates γ(x) and L = 4 is used for the positional encoding of viewing directions γ(d).

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) rely upon specialized volumetric rendering algorithms based on ray marching that are mismatched to the capabilities of widely deployed graphics hardware.
MobileNeRF represents a NeRF as a set of polygons with textures representing binary opacities and feature vectors.

Traditional rendering of MobileNeRF polygons with a z-buffer yields an image with features at every pixel, which are interpreted by a small, view-dependent MLP running in a fragment shader to produce a final pixel color.

MobileNeRF enables NeRFs to be rendered with the traditional polygon rasterization pipeline, which provides massive pixel-level parallelism, achieving interactive frame rates on a wide range of compute platforms, including mobile phones.

Traditional NeRF implementations use a volumetric rendering algorithm that evaluates a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions along the ray for each pixel in order to estimate and integrate density and radiance.
The traditional NeRF volumetric rendering process is far too slow for interactive visualization.
SNeRG (Sparse Neural Radiance Grids) precomputation and deferred rendering approach increases the rendering speed of NeRF by three orders of magnitude.

SNeRG still relies upon ray marching through a sparse voxel grid to produce the features for each pixel, and thus it cannot fully utilize the parallelism available in commodity graphics processing units (GPUs).
SNeRG requires a significant amount of GPU memory to store the volumetric textures, which prohibits it from running on common mobile devices.
MobileNeRF's rendering pipeline does not sample rays or sort polygons in depth order, and thus can model only binary opacities.
MobileNeRF is 10× faster than SNeRG with the same output quality on standard test scenes.

fact_fields.method: MobileNeRF vs SNeRG rendering speed comparison

claim_records.text: MobileNeRF consumes less memory by storing surface textures instead of volumetric textures, enabling the method to run on integrated GPUs with limited memory and power.
MobileNeRF runs on a web browser and is compatible with all devices tested, as its viewer is an HTML webpage.
MobileNeRF allows real-time manipulation of reconstructed objects/scenes, as they are simple triangle meshes.
MobileNeRF does not need reconstructed 3D geometry as input.
Point-based representations for view synthesis often result in a lack of 3D consistency because their convolutional post-processing runs independently per output frame.
Point-based view synthesis representations require powerful desktop GPUs and have not been demonstrated to run on a mobile device.
DefTet differentiably renders a tetrahedral grid with occupancy and color at each vertex, then composites the interpolated values at all intersected faces along a ray.
NVDiffRec combines differentiable marching tetrahedra with differentiable rasterization to perform full inverse rendering and extract triangle meshes, materials, and lighting from images.
Differentiable inverse-rendering representations like DefTet and NVDiffRec incur a significant loss in view-synthesis quality.
While real-time rendering is possible with simple lighting for differentiable inverse-rendering representations, global illumination (GI) is computationally infeasible on mobile hardware.
MobileNeRF simply caches the outgoing radiance, which does not need expensive compute to model GI effects, and also results in higher view-synthesis quality.
Rendering a NeRF involves evaluating a large neural network at multiple 3D locations per pixel, preventing real-time rendering.

methods: MobileNeRF vs SNeRG rendering speed comparison
claims: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) rely upon specialized volumetric rendering algorithms based on ray marching that are mismatched to the capabilities of widely deployed graphics hardware.
MobileNeRF represents a NeRF as a set of polygons with textures representing binary opacities and feature vectors.

Traditional rendering of MobileNeRF polygons with a z-buffer yields an image with features at every pixel, which are interpreted by a small, view-dependent MLP running in a fragment shader to produce a final pixel color.

MobileNeRF enables NeRFs to be rendered with the traditional polygon rasterization pipeline, which provides massive pixel-level parallelism, achieving interactive frame rates on a wide range of compute platforms, including mobile phones.

Traditional NeRF implementations use a volumetric rendering algorithm that evaluates a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions along the ray for each pixel in order to estimate and integrate density and radiance.
The traditional NeRF volumetric rendering process is far too slow for interactive visualization.
SNeRG (Sparse Neural Radiance Grids) precomputation and deferred rendering approach increases the rendering speed of NeRF by three orders of magnitude.

SNeRG still relies upon ray marching through a sparse voxel grid to produce the features for each pixel, and thus it cannot fully utilize the parallelism available in commodity graphics processing units (GPUs).
SNeRG requires a significant amount of GPU memory to store the volumetric textures, which prohibits it from running on common mobile devices.
MobileNeRF's rendering pipeline does not sample rays or sort polygons in depth order, and thus can model only binary opacities.
MobileNeRF is 10× faster than SNeRG with the same output quality on standard test scenes.
MobileNeRF consumes less memory by storing surface textures instead of volumetric textures, enabling the method to run on integrated GPUs with limited memory and power.
MobileNeRF runs on a web browser and is compatible with all devices tested, as its viewer is an HTML webpage.
MobileNeRF allows real-time manipulation of reconstructed objects/scenes, as they are simple triangle meshes.
MobileNeRF does not need reconstructed 3D geometry as input.
Point-based representations for view synthesis often result in a lack of 3D consistency because their convolutional post-processing runs independently per output frame.
Point-based view synthesis representations require powerful desktop GPUs and have not been demonstrated to run on a mobile device.
DefTet differentiably renders a tetrahedral grid with occupancy and color at each vertex, then composites the interpolated values at all intersected faces along a ray.
NVDiffRec combines differentiable marching tetrahedra with differentiable rasterization to perform full inverse rendering and extract triangle meshes, materials, and lighting from images.
Differentiable inverse-rendering representations like DefTet and NVDiffRec incur a significant loss in view-synthesis quality.
While real-time rendering is possible with simple lighting for differentiable inverse-rendering representations, global illumination (GI) is computationally infeasible on mobile hardware.
MobileNeRF simply caches the outgoing radiance, which does not need expensive compute to model GI effects, and also results in higher view-synthesis quality.
Rendering a NeRF involves evaluating a large neural network at multiple 3D locations per pixel, preventing real-time rendering.

claim_records.text: Progressive Volume Distillation (PVD) is a systematic distillation method that enables any-to-any conversions between different NeRF architectures, including MLP, sparse or low-rank tensors, hashtables and their compositions.

PVD performs distillation progressively on different levels of volume representations from shallower to deeper, and employs special treatment of density to address its specific numerical instability problem.

With PVD, an MLP-based NeRF model distilled from a hashtable-based Instant-NGP model achieves a 10×~20× faster speed than training the original NeRF from scratch, while achieving a superior level of synthesis quality.
PVD is validated empirically on the NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF and TanksAndTemples datasets.
Hashtable-based NeRF representations admit faster training and rendering, but their lack of clear geometric meaning hampers downstream tasks like spatial-relation-aware editing.

In the Family and Barn scenes from the TanksAndTemples dataset, a NeRF model distilled by PVD from an INGP teacher within 1.5 hours achieves improved synthesis quality compared to a NeRF model trained from scratch using 25 hours.
PVD uses loss on intermediate volume representations (including output of φ1*, color and density) alongside the final rendered RGB volume to accelerate distillation.
PVD employs a special treatment of the dynamic density volume range by clipping, which improves training stability and significantly improves synthesis quality.
Distillation from hashtable and VM-decomposition structures often helps boost student model synthesis quality and consumes less time than training from scratch.
PVD builds a block-wise distillation strategy to accelerate the training procedure based on a unified view of different NeRF architectures.

NeRF architectures including plain MLP, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, hashtables and their compositions each have particular sets of trade-offs between training speed, rendering speed, and downstream task suitability.
PVD empowers downstream applications to optimally adapt neural NeRF representations for the task at hand in a post hoc fashion.

claim_records.text: NeRF generates a volumetric representation called a radiance field that creates color and density for every point within the relevant 3D space, rather than directly restoring the whole 3D scene geometry.
NeRF uses an interpolation approach to produce new 3D reconstructed views of complicated scenes.
CAMPARI simultaneously learns a camera generator and an image generator, enabling use of complex camera distributions without manual tuning.
CAMPARI represents scenes through foreground and background decomposition, leading to 3D-consistent representations and accurate camera distribution recovery.
CAMPARI surpasses baseline models that heavily depend on accurately matched camera distributions, due to its performance without camera parameter tuning.
Pix2NeRF introduces a pipeline to generate NeRF from a single input image, built upon π-GAN which maps latent codes to radiance fields.
Pix2NeRF employs an unsupervised approach and can be trained with independent images, with potential applications in 3D avatar generation, novel view synthesis, and super-resolution.
Pix2NeRF is currently restricted to work with only one category per dataset, impeding its ability to generalize to new categories.
Pix2NeRF is built on top of π-GAN but is not limited to using π-GAN as its backbone; newer generative NeRF models such as EG3D may achieve better visual quality if used as a backbone.

NeRF uses a deep neural network to represent complex scenes in a fully connected, non-convolutional way, with input as a continuous 5D coordinate and output as volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.
The 5D coordinate space for NeRF includes three dimensions for spatial coordinates (x,y,z) and two dimensions for camera viewing angles (θ,φ).
NeRF uses classic volume rendering techniques to synthesize views and is optimized using a set of images with known camera poses.
NeRF introduces a positional encoding and a hierarchical sampling strategy to address the inefficiency of the basic implementation.
Using input viewing direction, NeRF can represent non-Lambertian effects such as specularities.
NeRF uses a separate neural continuous volume representation network for each scene.
This survey categorizes and compares recent NeRF advances according to their architectural designs, especially in the field of novel view synthesis.

claim_records.text: The introduced single-view volumetric reconstruction technique models unknown volumetric field distributions using an unconditional diffusion model trained on a novel benchmark dataset of 1,000 synthetically simulated volumetric density fields.

fact_fields.method: unconditional diffusion model for single-view volumetric reconstruction

claim_records.text: The neural diffusion model is trained on latent codes of a novel diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation.

A physically-based differentiable volume renderer is employed to provide gradients with respect to light transport in latent space, making reconstructions better aligned with observed data compared to classic NeRF approaches.
The diffusion model is trained on a dataset of 1,000 synthetically simulated volumetric density fields specifically consisting of cumulus clouds for the case study.

The proposed approach couples the renderer with the diffusion model to reconstruct radiance parameters using the prior for density distribution but not for appearance, so the 3D density field can be trained solely on the prior without requiring images of all possible backgrounds and light scattering effects.

fact_fields.method: diffusion prior guided physically-based differentiable volume renderer reconstruction

claim_records.text: The key contributions include a large database of 3D cumulus cloud-like density fields generated using numerical fluid simulation.
The key contributions include a 3D cloud decoder utilizing a novel diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation, trained jointly on a subset of the database.

fact_fields.method: 3D cloud decoder with diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation

claim_records.text: The key contributions include a novel Parametric Diffusion Posterior Sampling (PDPS) technique utilizing a shape-centric prior with a physically-based differentiable volume renderer.
To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first approach that integrates an unconditional diffusion model trained on volumetric density distributions with a differentiable volume renderer.

fact_fields.method: integrated unconditional diffusion model and differentiable volume renderer

claim_records.text: The proposed approach demonstrates potential across tasks including single- and multi-view reconstruction, and volume super-resolution.

fact_fields.method: light transport-aware diffusion posterior sampling for volumetric reconstruction

claim_records.text: Reconstructing the internal density distribution of highly dense volumes is widely considered nearly impossible due to high uncertainty in the light scattering process and presence of vanishing gradients, a limitation that can only be alleviated by incorporating prior information during reconstruction.

For complex volumetric materials such as clouds, smoke, or fire, the reconstruction problem becomes so ill-posed that it requires dozens, if not hundreds, of different views to adequately constrain object parameters.

claims: The introduced single-view volumetric reconstruction technique models unknown volumetric field distributions using an unconditional diffusion model trained on a novel benchmark dataset of 1,000 synthetically simulated volumetric density fields.
The neural diffusion model is trained on latent codes of a novel diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation.

A physically-based differentiable volume renderer is employed to provide gradients with respect to light transport in latent space, making reconstructions better aligned with observed data compared to classic NeRF approaches.
The diffusion model is trained on a dataset of 1,000 synthetically simulated volumetric density fields specifically consisting of cumulus clouds for the case study.

The proposed approach couples the renderer with the diffusion model to reconstruct radiance parameters using the prior for density distribution but not for appearance, so the 3D density field can be trained solely on the prior without requiring images of all possible backgrounds and light scattering effects.
The key contributions include a large database of 3D cumulus cloud-like density fields generated using numerical fluid simulation.
The key contributions include a 3D cloud decoder utilizing a novel diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation, trained jointly on a subset of the database.
The key contributions include a novel Parametric Diffusion Posterior Sampling (PDPS) technique utilizing a shape-centric prior with a physically-based differentiable volume renderer.
To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first approach that integrates an unconditional diffusion model trained on volumetric density distributions with a differentiable volume renderer.
The proposed approach demonstrates potential across tasks including single- and multi-view reconstruction, and volume super-resolution.

Reconstructing the internal density distribution of highly dense volumes is widely considered nearly impossible due to high uncertainty in the light scattering process and presence of vanishing gradients, a limitation that can only be alleviated by incorporating prior information during reconstruction.

For complex volumetric materials such as clouds, smoke, or fire, the reconstruction problem becomes so ill-posed that it requires dozens, if not hundreds, of different views to adequately constrain object parameters.

claim_records.text: Hyb-NeRF is a neural radiance field with a multi-resolution hybrid encoding that uses memory-efficient learnable positional features at coarse resolutions and hash-based feature grids at fine resolutions, achieving efficient neural modeling, fast rendering, and high-quality novel view synthesis.
Cone tracing-based features are embedded in the learnable positional encoding of Hyb-NeRF to eliminate encoding ambiguity and reduce aliasing artifacts.

fact_fields.method: cone tracing-based feature embedding in learnable positional encoding

claim_records.text: Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show Hyb-NeRF achieves faster rendering speed, better rendering quality, and lower memory footprint compared to previous state-of-the-art methods.
On the ficus scene in Blender, Hyb-NeRF with 16.4M parameters achieves 35.85 PSNR and 0.986 SSIM, compared to JNGP with 24.4M parameters achieving 33.23 PSNR and 0.981 SSIM.
All Hyb-NeRF models can reconstruct high-quality radiance fields in 9 minutes.

The smallest Hyb-NeRF model with 8.4M trainable parameters takes 4 minutes to achieve better rendering quality than state-of-the-art methods while requiring substantially less memory than previous and concurrent voxel-based methods.

Hyb-NeRF concatenates coarse-level learnable positional features with fine-level multi-resolution feature grids for multi-resolution scene representation, yielding detailed 3D reconstructions and high-quality rendering.
NeRF requires hundreds of network evaluations per pixel to approximate a volume rendering integral, making it slow to train.
Caching NeRFs into explicit data structures can effectively enhance rendering speed but at the cost of higher memory usage.

fact_fields.method: explicit data structure caching for NeRF

claim_records.text: Hash-based multi-resolution grid representation is fast to train and well suited to fast operation, but trainable features at coarse resolution levels have lower resolutions and are less compressed than feature grids at fine resolution levels, resulting in limited representation power and low memory efficiency.

claim_records.text: NeRF's rendering procedure samples a scene with a single ray per pixel and may produce renderings that are excessively blurred or aliased when training or testing images observe scene content at different resolutions.

The straightforward solution of supersampling by rendering with multiple rays per pixel is impractical for NeRF, because rendering each ray requires querying a multilayer perceptron hundreds of times.

fact_fields.method: supersampling with multiple rays per pixel

claim_records.text: mip-NeRF extends NeRF to represent the scene at a continuously-valued scale by efficiently rendering anti-aliased conical frustums instead of rays.
mip-NeRF reduces objectionable aliasing artifacts and significantly improves NeRF's ability to represent fine details, while also being 7% faster than NeRF and half the size.
Compared to NeRF, mip-NeRF reduces average error rates by 17% on the dataset presented with NeRF.
Compared to NeRF, mip-NeRF reduces average error rates by 60% on a challenging multiscale variant of the NeRF dataset.
Mip-NeRF is able to match the accuracy of a brute-force supersampled NeRF on the multiscale dataset while being 22x faster.

Mip-NeRF reasons about the 3D conical frustum defined by a camera pixel, and featurizes these conical frustums with integrated positional encoding (IPE) by approximating the frustum with a multivariate Gaussian and computing the closed-form integral E[γ(x)] over positional encodings of coordinates within the Gaussian.
When training images observe scene content at multiple resolutions, renderings from the recovered NeRF appear excessively blurred in close-up views and contain aliasing artifacts in distant views.

Mip-NeRF's scale-aware structure allows merging the separate 'coarse' and 'fine' MLPs used by NeRF for hierarchical sampling into a single MLP, making mip-NeRF slightly faster than NeRF (~7%) and having half as many parameters.
A NeRF trained on full-resolution images produces photorealistic renderings at new view locations only at the resolution or scale of the training images.
Adjusting camera intrinsics to reduce image resolution for a NeRF trained on full-resolution images results in renderings that exhibit severe aliasing.
Training a NeRF on multi-resolution images ameliorates aliasing issues slightly but results in poor quality renderings across scales: blur at full resolution, and 'jaggies' at low resolutions.
Mip-NeRF trained on multi-resolution images is capable of producing photorealistic renderings across different scales.

claim_records.text: Fourier PlenOctrees suffer from artifacts introduced by the involved compression when combined with recent state-of-the-art techniques for training static per-frame NeRF models.

The proposed novel density encoding adapts the Fourier-based compression to the characteristics of the transfer function used by the underlying volume rendering procedure and leads to a substantial reduction of artifacts in the dynamic model.

fact_fields.method: novel density encoding for Fourier PlenOctrees

claim_records.text: An augmentation of the training data is proposed that relaxes the periodicity assumption of the Fourier compression used in Fourier PlenOctrees.
PlenOctrees use a hierarchical octree structure of density and view-dependent radiance in terms of spherical harmonics (SH) to entirely avoid network evaluations.
Instant-NGP incorporated a multi-resolution hash encoding to significantly accelerate the training of neural models including NeRF.
Plenoxels stored SH and opacity values within a sparse voxel grid.
TensoRF factorized dense voxel grids into multiple low-rank components.

Fourier PlenOctrees (FPO) relaxed the limitation of ordinary PlenOctrees to only capture static scenes in a hierarchical manner by combining it with the Fourier transform which enables handling time-variant density and SH-based radiance in an efficient way.
During FPO construction, compression is performed on encoded densities σ′ = ecomp(elog(σ)), where the encoding consists of a component-dependent part and a logarithmic part.
The proposed encoding allows for a better reconstruction of the original densities without any fine-tuning than can be achieved with only the DFT and IDFT as proposed for FPOs.

fact_fields.method: proposed component-dependent + logarithmic density encoding vs DFT/IDFT-only FPO

claim_records.text: Non-negative density values σ are encoded logarithmically using elog(σ) = log(σ + 1) before applying the DFT, with the shift by 1 chosen so that elog remains a non-negative function for non-negative input densities with elog(0) = 0.
The logarithmic density encoding maps larger density values closer together while keeping smaller values almost unchanged, focusing approximation on densities near or equal to zero.
The encoded density sequences are easier to approximate with a low-frequency Fourier basis exploiting the properties of the transfer function.
The L2-error in fine-tuning is allowed to be larger for encoded high density values than without logarithmic encoding, focusing optimization on the more important parts of the reconstruction.
During rendering, the inverse of the logarithmic encoding elog(σ) = log(σ + 1) is applied after the IDFT to project densities back to their original range.

methods: novel density encoding for Fourier PlenOctrees

claim_records.text: NerfDiff addresses the blurry rendering issue under severe occlusion by distilling the knowledge of a 3D-aware conditional diffusion model (CDM) into NeRF through synthesizing and refining a set of virtual views at test time.
NerfDiff uses a novel NeRF-guided distillation algorithm that simultaneously generates 3D consistent virtual views from the CDM samples, and finetunes the NeRF based on the improved virtual views.
NerfDiff significantly outperforms existing NeRF-based and geometry-free approaches on challenging datasets including ShapeNet, ABO, and Clevr3D.

claims: Existing NeRF-based single-image novel view synthesis approaches condition neural radiance fields on local image features, projecting points to the input image plane, and aggregating 2D features to perform volume rendering.

NerfDiff addresses the blurry rendering issue under severe occlusion by distilling the knowledge of a 3D-aware conditional diffusion model (CDM) into NeRF through synthesizing and refining a set of virtual views at test time.
NerfDiff uses a novel NeRF-guided distillation algorithm that simultaneously generates 3D consistent virtual views from the CDM samples, and finetunes the NeRF based on the improved virtual views.
NerfDiff significantly outperforms existing NeRF-based and geometry-free approaches on challenging datasets including ShapeNet, ABO, and Clevr3D.

claim_records.text: The rendering scheme in neural radiance field (NeRF) is effective in rendering a pixel by casting a ray into the scene.
NeRF yields blurred rendering results when the training images are captured at non-uniform scales.
NeRF produces aliasing artifacts if the test images are taken in distant views.
Mip-NeRF proposes a multiscale representation as a conical frustum to encode scale information.
Mip-NeRF is only suitable for offline rendering since it relies on integrated positional encoding (IPE) to query a multilayer perceptron (MLP).
Mip-VoG is an explicit multiscale representation with a deferred architecture for real-time anti-aliasing rendering.
Mip-VoG includes a density Mip-VoG for scene geometry and a feature Mip-VoG with a small MLP for view-dependent color.
Mip-VoG encodes scene scale using the level of detail (LOD) derived from ray differentials.
Mip-VoG uses quadrilinear interpolation to map a queried 3D location to its features and density from two neighboring downsampled voxel grids.
Mip-VoG is the first approach to offer multiscale training and real-time anti-aliasing rendering simultaneously.
Experiments on multiscale datasets show that Mip-VoG outperforms state-of-the-art real-time rendering baselines.

claim_records.text: pixelNeRF is a learning framework that predicts a continuous neural scene representation conditioned on one or few input images.
pixelNeRF introduces an architecture that conditions a NeRF on image inputs in a fully convolutional manner.

The fully convolutional conditioning design allows the network to be trained across multiple scenes to learn a scene prior, enabling feed-forward novel view synthesis from a sparse set of views as few as one.
Leveraging NeRF's volume rendering approach, the pixelNeRF model can be trained directly from images with no explicit 3D supervision.

claim_records.text: CLIP-NeRF is a multi-modal 3D object manipulation method for neural radiance fields that leverages the joint language-image embedding space of the CLIP model.
CLIP-NeRF allows manipulating NeRF using either a short text prompt or an exemplar image.
CLIP-NeRF introduces a disentangled conditional NeRF architecture that allows individual control over both shape and appearance.
In CLIP-NeRF, shape conditioning is achieved by applying a learned deformation field to the positional encoding, and color conditioning is deferred to the volumetric rendering stage.
CLIP-NeRF designs two code mappers that take a CLIP embedding as input and update the latent codes to reflect the targeted editing.
The CLIP-NeRF code mappers are trained with a CLIP-based matching loss to ensure manipulation accuracy.
CLIP-NeRF proposes an inverse optimization method that accurately projects an input image to the latent codes for manipulation to enable editing on real images.
CLIP-NeRF is evaluated via extensive experiments on a variety of text prompts and exemplar images, and provides an intuitive interface for interactive editing.

claim_records.text: NeRF trains a deep network to map 5D input coordinates representing spatial location and viewing direction into a volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance.
NeRF is only applicable to static scenes where the same spatial location can be queried from different images.

D-NeRF extends neural radiance fields to a dynamic domain, allowing reconstruction and rendering of novel images of objects under rigid and non-rigid motions from a single camera moving around the scene.

D-NeRF treats time as an additional input and splits learning into two stages: one encoding the scene into a canonical space, and another mapping the canonical representation into the deformed scene at a particular time.
Both mappings in D-NeRF are simultaneously learned using fully-connected networks.
After training, D-NeRF can render novel images while controlling both the camera view and the time variable, and thus the object movement.
D-NeRF demonstrates effectiveness on scenes with objects under rigid, articulated and non-rigid motions.

claim_records.text: NeRF has emerged as a powerful representation for novel view synthesis due to its simplicity and state-of-the-art performance.
NeRF can produce photorealistic renderings of unseen viewpoints when many input views are available.
NeRF performance drops significantly when the number of input views is reduced.
The majority of artifacts in sparse input NeRF scenarios are caused by errors in estimated scene geometry and by divergent behavior at the start of training.
RegNeRF regularizes the geometry and appearance of patches rendered from unobserved viewpoints, and anneals the ray sampling space during training.
RegNeRF additionally uses a normalizing flow model to regularize the color of unobserved viewpoints.
RegNeRF outperforms other methods that optimize over a single scene.
In many cases, RegNeRF also outperforms conditional models that are extensively pre-trained on large multi-view datasets.

claim_records.text: NeRF and its variants require a lengthy training time ranging from hours to days for reconstructing a single scene.
The proposed direct voxel grid optimization approach achieves NeRF-comparable quality and converges from scratch in less than 15 minutes with a single GPU.
The proposed representation uses a density voxel grid for scene geometry and a feature voxel grid with a shallow network for complex view-dependent appearance.
Post-activation interpolation on voxel density is capable of producing sharp surfaces in lower grid resolution.
Imposing several priors robustifies the direct voxel density optimization process, which is otherwise prone to suboptimal geometry solutions.
