input.query: Explain the foundational NeRF representation and differentiable volume-rendering formulation.
input.survey:
# Foundational NeRF: A Continuous 5D Radiance Field with Differentiable Volume Rendering

## Abstract

Foundational NeRF represents one scene as a continuous coordinate-based MLP field mapping 3D position and viewing direction to emitted RGB color and volume density. Density depends on position alone, supporting view-consistent occupancy and occlusion, while color may depend on viewing direction to represent view-dependent appearance. Camera rays are evaluated at sampled points, and differentiable emission-absorption volume rendering composites local colors using interval opacity and accumulated transmittance. Photometric loss between rendered and observed pixels, with known poses, back-propagates through this quadrature to optimize the MLP. Positional encoding and coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling are practical components that improve high-frequency detail and allocate more samples to contributing ray segments, but the baseline remains a per-scene continuous neural field rather than an explicit mesh, voxel model, or feed-forward reconstructor. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:942ee00c2fdd] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:297d1862724d]

## Introduction

This review groups the foundational NeRF pipeline around three linked choices rather than treating every later NeRF variant as the same method: the scene representation, the ray-based rendering operator, and the image-supervised optimization loop. The scope here is the original NeRF formulation for novel view synthesis: learn a continuous volumetric scene function from posed photographs and render new camera views by integrating density and color along rays. Later systems that bake fields into voxels, polygons, meshes, hash grids, or other acceleration structures address efficiency, scale, aliasing, editing, or deployment objectives and should not be conflated with the baseline representation. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:01320e9d4bc0] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f]

At the representation level, NeRF defines a scene as a continuous 5D vector-valued function. Its input is a 3D spatial location x=(x,y,z) and a viewing direction, written in the original paper as (θ,φ) and implemented as a 3D Cartesian unit vector d; its output is an emitted RGB color c=(r,g,b) and a volume density σ. A multilayer perceptron FΘ approximates the mapping (x,d)→(c,σ), with separate treatment of geometry and appearance: density is predicted from position alone, while color may depend on both position and viewing direction. This design encourages multiview-consistent occupancy while allowing view-dependent appearance such as specular effects. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a]

For rendering, NeRF casts a camera ray r(t)=o+td and evaluates the network at sample locations along that ray. Classical volume rendering accumulates the samples into a pixel color: each sample contributes its color weighted by its local opacity, (1−exp(−σ_iδ_i)), and by accumulated transmittance T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jδ_j), where δ_i is the distance between adjacent samples. The resulting discrete sum is Ĉ(r)=Σ_i T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i))c_i, with a background term when ray termination is modeled. This quadrature is a piecewise-constant approximation to the continuous emission-absorption integral and is differentiable, so gradients from rendered pixels can update the MLP weights. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a]

Training therefore requires only images and known camera poses in the original setup: NeRF renders rays from the training viewpoints, compares predicted colors with observed pixel colors, and back-propagates the rendering loss through the compositing and network evaluations. The original method also uses positional encoding to expose high-frequency coordinate variation and a coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling strategy: a coarse network estimates sample weights, and a fine network receives additional samples drawn from the normalized coarse weights so that more evaluations concentrate where the ray is expected to contribute. These components make the foundational model a per-scene optimized continuous field, not a generic mesh or an explicit voxel reconstruction. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54]

## Background and Method Taxonomy

For this review, the organizing choice is a pipeline-based grouping: representation, rendering operator, and optimization objective. This grouping is used to explain the foundational NeRF formulation; it is not a universal taxonomy of all neural-rendering methods, nor is it a paper-proposed classification. Under this grouping, the defining relationship is that a continuous field supplies density and color at queried coordinates, differentiable volume rendering composites those samples along camera rays, and the resulting pixel error supervises the field. Later methods can still be NeRF-like if they preserve this field-to-ray-compositing relationship, even when they change the data structure or sampling strategy. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06]

The first classification criterion is what represents the scene. The original NeRF uses a per-scene, coordinate-based MLP: the network parameters encode a continuous function over 3D position and viewing direction rather than storing colors on an explicit mesh or a fixed voxel grid. This separates it from representations whose primary scene store is polygons, textured meshes, voxel textures, hash tables, sparse tensors, or other explicit feature structures. Such structures may be used to accelerate, bake, distill, or rasterize a NeRF-derived model, but they are different implementation choices from the original continuous MLP field. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce]

The second criterion is how geometry and appearance are factorized within the representation. In foundational NeRF, density is constrained to be a function of position only, whereas emitted RGB color can depend on position and viewing direction. That distinction is important: density supplies the view-invariant occupancy used by transmittance and occlusion, while directional color permits non-Lambertian or specular appearance. Methods that replace the view-dependent color shader with diffuse texture plus residuals, surface texture plus view-aware lobes, reflection-ray tracing, or learned feature decoding alter the appearance model; they should not be read as changing the original density-color distinction by itself. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54] [E:arxiv:2311.09806:abstract:claim:2225f1f6f32b]

The third criterion is the rendering integral and its discretization. Foundational NeRF casts one ray through each pixel, queries the field at points along that ray, and alpha-composites colors using local opacity and accumulated transmittance. This is emission-absorption volume rendering, not direct z-buffered surface rendering. A method that rasterizes textured polygons or mesh primitives and then invokes a small shader changes the primary visibility mechanism, even if it retains view-dependent color or was trained from a NeRF. Conversely, mip-NeRF remains closely related to the original ray-based formulation but replaces infinitesimal ray samples with anti-aliased conical frustums to encode scale, addressing blur and aliasing rather than replacing volume compositing with rasterization. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe]

The fourth criterion is sampling scope. Hierarchical volume sampling in the original NeRF is an efficiency allocation mechanism inside the same rendering formulation: a coarse network evaluates stratified samples, its normalized compositing weights define a piecewise-constant distribution, and inverse-transform sampling adds fine samples in regions expected to affect the pixel. The fine result still uses volume rendering over the union of samples. This differs from deployment-oriented acceleration schemes that bake the field, use deferred shaders, rasterize polygons, employ explicit level-of-detail structures, or partition large scenes; those change storage, hardware use, or visibility computation, whereas coarse-to-fine sampling changes where the MLP is queried. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719] [E:arxiv:2310.13263:abstract:claim:d66087edc431]

The final criterion is supervision and applicability. The original setup optimizes one scene from multiple posed images by comparing rendered and observed colors; it does not require explicit 3D labels in that formulation. Feed-forward or conditional NeRFs, single-image reconstruction systems, and generative diffusion-coupled methods introduce learned priors or additional conditioning and therefore solve a different data-regime problem from the original per-scene optimization. Likewise, methods focused on multiscale anti-aliasing, mobile frame rate, urban scale, geometry extraction, editing, or architecture conversion are related along selected pipeline dimensions but have distinct objectives; their results cannot be treated as direct rankings unless datasets, hardware, training views, and metrics are matched. ## Representative Methods

The foundational NeRF method represents one scene with a coordinate-based multilayer perceptron rather than an explicit mesh, voxel array, or point cloud. The network is a continuous 5D scene function FΘ(x,d)→(c,σ): x is a 3D position, d is the viewing direction represented in implementation as a three-dimensional Cartesian unit vector, c is emitted RGB color, and σ is volume density. Thus, every queried point in the scene volume returns local appearance and opacity-like density; the learned weights Θ are optimized for that scene from posed images. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] Geometry and appearance are deliberately factorized inside the MLP. Density is restricted to depend only on 3D position x, so the same spatial location has one occupancy field across viewpoints. Color is allowed to depend on both x and viewing direction d, which gives the model a mechanism for view-dependent non-Lambertian appearance such as specular highlights. In the original architecture, eight fully connected ReLU layers with 256 channels process position and output σ plus a 256-dimensional feature; that feature is concatenated with the ray direction and passed through an additional fully connected ReLU layer with 128 channels to predict RGB. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54]

A camera ray is written as r(t)=o+td, with origin o and unit direction d. NeRF evaluates the field at coordinates sampled along this ray and turns those local field values into one pixel color. This makes the representation volumetric: visibility is not decided by intersecting a single surface, but by accumulating emission and occlusion through the density distribution along the ray. The same ray-sampling procedure is used during training and novel-view rendering; only the camera pose and image pixels change. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] The continuous physical model is an emission-absorption volume integral. For a ray r(t), color is C(r)=∫ c(r(t),d) σ(r(t)) T(t) dt, where T(t)=exp(−∫_0^t σ(r(s))ds) is accumulated transmittance: the probability that light traveling from distance t toward the camera has not been stopped by earlier density. In this formulation, σ acts as an absorption coefficient or density field, while c is the radiance emitted at that location toward direction d. A finite far-boundary term can account for light entering from the background. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] NeRF approximates the integral numerically at N samples along each ray. If t_i is a sample, δ_i is the interval width to the next sample, σ_i and c_i are the network outputs at that sample, and T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jδ_j), then the discrete alpha-composited color is Ĉ(r)=Σ_{i=1}^{N} T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i))c_i, plus the background contribution weighted by remaining transmittance where used. The factor α_i=1−exp(−σ_iδ_i) is the local opacity assigned to the interval, while T_i is the product of earlier interval transmittances. This quadrature treats the field as approximately constant over each sampled neighborhood. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180]

Differentiability is the key property that connects rendering to representation learning. The sampled colors, densities, interval widths, transmittance products, and final pixel color form a computation graph through which a photometric rendering loss can be back-propagated to the MLP parameters. The original optimization compares colors rendered from training camera rays with observed ground-truth pixel colors; no explicit 3D geometry labels are required by this basic formulation. In other words, multi-view image consistency, mediated by known camera poses, supervises the continuous density and radiance function. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] The original implementation does not feed raw coordinates directly to the network in its high-frequency formulation. Positional encoding maps spatial and directional coordinates into sinusoidal features at multiple frequencies. This component addresses the difficulty that ordinary MLPs can have representing high-frequency color and geometry variation from low-dimensional coordinate inputs. It is therefore part of the practical NeRF mechanism for sharp view synthesis, but it is distinct from the density-color field definition and from the volume-rendering equation. [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:942ee00c2fdd]

Naive dense quadrature is expensive because the network is evaluated at many points along every pixel ray, including empty space and regions hidden behind visible content. Foundational NeRF therefore uses hierarchical volume sampling with two networks, called coarse and fine. The coarse network first evaluates N_c stratified samples along a ray. Its rendered color is rewritten as a weighted sum, with sample weights w_i=T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i)); after normalization, these weights define a piecewise-constant probability distribution over ray segments. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:297d1862724d] NeRF then draws N_f additional samples from the coarse distribution by inverse transform sampling and evaluates the fine network at the union of the original and second-stage samples. This places more network evaluations in segments that the coarse pass expects to contribute to the pixel, while still rendering the final color with the same differentiable volume-compositing equation over all N_c+N_f samples. The paper describes this as allocating samples according to expected effect rather than treating each sample as an independent Monte Carlo estimate of the whole integral. It is an internal sampling strategy, not a replacement of the continuous field with an explicit spatial data structure. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:297d1862724d]

The method’s contribution is therefore the combination of three ideas: a continuous 5D neural field with position-only density and directional color, classical differentiable volume rendering over ray samples, and pose-supervised per-scene optimization, made practical by positional encoding and coarse-to-fine sampling. The reported claim in the original paper is that this pipeline synthesizes novel views of complex scenes more faithfully than prior neural rendering and view-synthesis methods evaluated there. That evidence supports the original method’s role as a learned view-synthesis representation; it does not by itself establish fast rendering, explicit geometry extraction, or feed-forward reconstruction across scenes. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] The applicability boundary of foundational NeRF is narrower than that of the broader NeRF family. It optimizes a separate network for each scene, requires training images with known camera poses in the original setup, and renders by querying an MLP many times per ray. Consequently, later methods that condition a NeRF on input images, distill between MLP and explicit-grid architectures, bake features into voxels, rasterize polygons, trace reflection rays, or model surfaces and textures are modifying the data regime, representation store, rendering path, or appearance model; they should not be described as merely repeating the original 5D MLP and ray-marching mechanism. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:42d03ceacbbb] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f] Two later comparisons clarify what is and is not changed in the foundational formulation. Mip-NeRF retains the neural-field and anti-aliased volume-rendering lineage but queries conical frustums with integrated positional encoding so that scale-dependent blur and aliasing can be modeled; it targets a sampling limitation of one ray per pixel. MobileNeRF instead changes deployment-oriented visibility by representing a baked NeRF with textured polygons and using z-buffer rasterization followed by a small view-dependent MLP. These are related NeRF-derived systems, but neither is the same mechanism as the original continuous MLP evaluated at point samples along camera rays. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719]

## Comparative Evidence Analysis

The experimental comparison in this review is organized by the same pipeline dimensions used above—representation, ray-sampled differentiable rendering, and optimization—rather than by treating all later NeRF-derived systems as one benchmark family. The original NeRF evidence establishes that a per-scene MLP field, volume rendering, posed-image supervision, positional encoding, and hierarchical sampling can outperform the neural rendering and view-synthesis baselines evaluated in that paper. The selected later papers provide evidence about different objectives, such as anti-aliasing, deployment speed, architecture conversion, or surface rendering; their numbers are not a matched ranking against foundational NeRF unless dataset, task, hardware, views, and metrics are the same. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f] The foundational NeRF experiment is a novel-view-synthesis experiment: optimize a separate continuous 5D network for each scene from a sparse set of posed input images, render held-out camera rays by differentiable volume compositing, and compare rendered RGB pixels with ground-truth images. Its central quantitative claim in the source is state-of-the-art view synthesis on the complex scenes used in the original study. The frozen source excerpts supplied here do not include the paper's full per-dataset metric table, so this section should not invent PSNR, SSIM, or LPIPS values for the original benchmark. What is directly supported is the comparison direction and the evaluation mechanism, not an unstated numerical score. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:56629e322cde] Within the original method, the coarse and fine networks are compared under the same rendering equation but with different sample allocations. The coarse network evaluates N_c stratified samples and forms weights w_i=T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i)); normalized weights define a piecewise-constant PDF, inverse-transform sampling adds N_f samples, and the fine network renders from the union of N_c+N_f samples. This is therefore not a comparison between two unrelated rendering models: the fine stage uses the coarse stage's density-weighted estimate to place more queries in visible or otherwise contributing regions. The supported benefit is better allocation of ray samples; the excerpt does not provide a standalone coarse-versus-fine PSNR table. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:297d1862724d] The discrete rendering experiment also exposes the main cost dimension. Each pixel requires a camera ray, and each ray requires many MLP evaluations at sample positions; dense quadrature repeatedly queries free space and occluded regions that contribute little or nothing to the final color. Hierarchical sampling mitigates this waste inside NeRF by biasing later samples toward expected content, but it does not change the fundamental requirement of network evaluation along rays. Consequently, the original method's evidence supports high-quality offline view synthesis more directly than interactive rendering; later speed claims must be attributed to their changed representations or rendering pipelines. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719]

Mip-NeRF is the closest selected comparison on the rendering-sampling dimension because it preserves the neural radiance-field lineage but changes the query primitive from an infinitesimal point sample along a single ray to an anti-aliased conical frustum encoding continuous scale. On the dataset presented with NeRF, mip-NeRF is reported to reduce average error rates by 17% relative to NeRF; on a challenging multiscale variant introduced by mip-NeRF, the reduction is 60%. It is also reported to be about 7% faster than NeRF, half the size, and capable of matching brute-force supersampled NeRF accuracy on the multiscale dataset while being 22× faster. These results are specific to the scale/anti-aliasing setting and should not be generalized as ordinary fixed-resolution superiority. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:b14753cf9c18] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:section:abstract:3:97643459cce9:claim:4cdea39204ef] The mip-NeRF comparison also clarifies why supersampling is not an apples-to-apples baseline for interactive use. Casting multiple rays per pixel can reduce aliasing, but runtime generally scales with the supersampling rate because every extra ray still requires hundreds of MLP queries in NeRF. Mip-NeRF's reported 22× speed advantage is relative to brute-force supersampled NeRF on the authors' multiscale dataset, not relative to every explicit-grid or rasterization accelerator. Likewise, its 7% speed gain over NeRF and half-as-large model arise from integrating coarse and fine sampling into a single MLP in that system; they are not properties of the original coarse-plus-fine NeRF architecture. The authors state that mip-NeRF relies on integrated positional encoding and MLP queries and is therefore suited to offline rendering, whereas Mip-VoG targets simultaneous multiscale training and real-time anti-aliased rendering. Their reported result is superiority over state-of-the-art real-time rendering baselines on multiscale datasets; the supplied excerpt does not provide matched metric values or a direct head-to-head runtime table against original NeRF, so no numerical ranking can be reconstructed here. MobileNeRF represents a baked NeRF as textured polygons carrying binary opacities and feature vectors; z-buffer rasterization produces per-pixel features, and a small view-dependent MLP in a fragment shader decodes the final color. Its evidence targets interactive frame rates across commodity platforms, including mobile devices, by exploiting standard polygon rasterization rather than specialized ray marching. This comparison supports a hardware-pipeline and latency objective, but the selected excerpt does not supply a common dataset metric table against the original NeRF implementation. Architecture-conversion evidence is also distinct from view-synthesis benchmarking. Baked voxel, polygon, hash-grid, mesh-primitive, and distillation systems report speed, memory, platform, or conversion benefits after changing the storage or visibility pipeline. Because their tasks, datasets, baselines, hardware, and output objectives differ, the available excerpts do not support a single global ranking; the defensible comparison is that the foundational formulation is the common differentiable rendering baseline, while later numbers measure specific modifications under specific experimental conditions. ## Limitations and Open Problems

The main computational limitation follows directly from the foundational rendering equation. NeRF must cast a ray for each pixel and evaluate an MLP at hundreds of sample positions along that ray to estimate and integrate density and radiance; free space and occluded regions can still be queried repeatedly. Coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling allocates more samples to segments expected to contribute, but it remains a ray-marching, multi-evaluation process rather than a constant-time surface lookup. The implication is that the original formulation is well matched to offline per-scene optimization and high-quality view synthesis, but its basic rendering path is too expensive for interactive visualization without changing sampling, storage, or the visibility pipeline. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719]

A second limitation is scale and aliasing. Foundational NeRF samples a scene with a single ray per pixel, so it can produce blurred results when training images observe content at nonuniform scales and aliasing or jagged artifacts when test views are distant. Simply casting multiple rays per pixel is a direct supersampling remedy, but in NeRF it multiplies an already large MLP-query cost and is generally impractical outside offline rendering. Mip-NeRF's scale-aware conical frustums and later explicit mip voxel grids are evidence that this is a real limitation of point-ray sampling; they also show that anti-aliasing and real-time deployment may require separate architectural changes. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:section:abstract:3:97643459cce9:claim:4cdea39204ef] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:3fee88baf342]

The continuous density field is a rendering representation, not by itself an unambiguous explicit surface reconstruction. NeRF is supervised through rendered color, and later analysis identifies a shape-radiance ambiguity: view-dependent radiance and inferred geometry can interact so that image fidelity does not necessarily determine one unique geometric explanation. This matters when the desired output is a mesh, accurate normals, animation, or manipulation rather than a novel-view image. Methods that normalize view dependence or use explicit surface and texture models target that geometry ambiguity, but they add assumptions or components not present in the original color-supervised volume-rendering setup. [E:arxiv:2010.07492:abstract:claim:a215bcfde7b2] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:249ec5b6f7a4] [E:arxiv:2311.09806:abstract:claim:2225f1f6f32b]

View-dependent color is both a capability and a modeling boundary. Allowing RGB to depend on position and viewing direction lets foundational NeRF represent non-Lambertian effects such as specular highlights, but highly shiny scenes can contain quickly changing appearance and reflections of nearby content that a single outgoing-radiance MLP may model only at substantial network cost. Reflection-ray methods address this by tracing additional rays through the field and decoding traced features with a smaller network. That evidence should be read as a limitation of the original appearance model under strong specularity, not as a failure of density-based volume rendering in general. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2405.14871:abstract:claim:1aed0f9d756b] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:314ce4ef2d54]

The original NeRF also has a data-regime limitation: it optimizes a separate MLP for each scene from posed training images. It is not a feed-forward model that reconstructs an unseen scene from one image, and the basic formulation assumes camera poses are available for photometric supervision. PixelNeRF and conditional or diffusion-distilled systems introduce image features, learned cross-scene priors, or generated virtual views to operate from one or a sparse set of inputs. These methods relax the original data requirement, but they change the learning problem and should not be interpreted as the same per-scene optimization result. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:42d03ceacbbb] [E:arxiv:2302.10109:abstract:claim:370fdae62ed9]

Memory and hardware compatibility create a separate trade-off when NeRFs are accelerated. Caching or baking a continuous field into sparse voxels can improve rendering speed, but it raises storage or GPU-memory use; SNeRG's precomputed sparse grid, for example, accelerates deferred rendering yet still ray-marches volumetric textures and requires significant GPU memory. MobileNeRF instead moves visibility to textured polygons and z-buffer rasterization so commodity graphics pipelines and mobile GPUs can be used. These are deployment solutions, not free speedups of the original MLP: they alter the representation store and often require baking or a deferred shader. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:72ae3e030d32] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce]

Large scenes intensify both computation and organization costs. A single monolithic ray-marched field does not naturally map to the culling, level-of-detail, and rasterization mechanisms used for urban-scale interactive graphics. Systems such as UE4-NeRF partition scenes and combine optimized mesh-like proxies with game-engine rasterization, while deformable neural mesh primitives seek rasterization efficiency and lower peak memory for urban rendering. Their speed and memory claims depend on those primitives, partitioning, level-of-detail, and engine integration; they do not establish that the unmodified foundational NeRF has the same scalability. [E:arxiv:2310.13263:abstract:claim:d66087edc431] [E:arxiv:2307.10776:abstract:claim:e4c55e718898] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:d2f57abe0719]

Architecture choice also involves downstream trade-offs beyond average rendering quality. Plain MLPs provide a continuous coordinate field with comparatively clear functional structure, whereas hash tables, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, tri-planes, and hybrid encodings can train or render faster but may have less clear geometric meaning or different memory profiles. PVD's any-to-any distillation and Hyb-NeRF's coarse-to-fine hybrid encoding are responses to this fragmentation: practitioners may convert or combine representations for editing, training speed, rendering speed, or memory. The limitation is that no single store in the selected evidence dominates all of these objectives simultaneously. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:4:97facdcc473c:claim:cec90d41fbf0] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:95df0ad0b144]

The physical scope of the basic emission-absorption model should also be distinguished from full participating-media light transport. The NeRF integral accumulates locally emitted color and density along a camera ray; it does not, in its foundational form, solve multiple scattering or global illumination in a general volumetric medium. Work on volumetric clouds uses a physically based differentiable volume renderer and diffusion prior to provide gradients for multiple-scattering light transport, explicitly contrasting that setting with classic NeRF approaches. Thus, strong scattering media are outside the applicability boundary of the original local radiance-and-density formulation. [E:arxiv:2501.05226:abstract:claim:c3f096e7de3c] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a]

Taken together, these limitations should be attributed to specific parts of the pipeline rather than used as a blanket claim that neural radiance fields are unsuitable. The original formulation's core open trade-offs are: many MLP evaluations per ray, point-sample aliasing under scale change, geometry ambiguity under photometric and view-dependent supervision, per-scene posed-image training, and difficulty matching commodity rasterization hardware without baking or restructuring the field. Later evidence shows that anti-aliasing, feed-forward priors, surface models, reflection tracing, explicit grids, polygons, mesh primitives, and architecture distillation can address individual constraints, but each changes assumptions and introduces its own quality, memory, physical-accuracy, editing, or deployment trade-off. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:abstract:claim:0646fb00e3ce] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:3a797c27b73f]

## Conclusion

The core answer is that NeRF combines a 5D neural radiance field with classical differentiable volume rendering: the MLP supplies density and color at queried ray coordinates, transmittance-weighted alpha compositing forms each pixel, and posed-image error supervises the field without explicit 3D labels. The discrete estimator is Ĉ(r)=Σ_i T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i))c_i, with optional remaining-transmittance background weighting. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:3_neural_radiance_field_scene_representation:0:e6a7774107f3:claim:f3aee83c7d23] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:5_2_hierarchical_volume_sampling:0:7c4cd481bcd3:claim:e2c3652cc180]

The main trade-off is expressive, image-based view synthesis against sampling cost: hierarchical sampling concentrates MLP evaluations where coarse weights indicate contribution, but the original method still requires many network queries per ray and is best understood as offline per-scene optimization. Its point-ray formulation also leaves scale aliasing, geometry ambiguity, and deployment acceleration to later modified architectures rather than being solved by the baseline representation itself. claims: The NeRF method represents a scene using a fully-connected (non-convolutional) deep network that takes a single continuous 5D coordinate (spatial location (x,y,z) and viewing direction (θ, φ)) as input and outputs volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.
NeRF synthesizes novel views by querying 5D coordinates along camera rays and using classic volume rendering techniques to project output colors and densities into an image.
Because volume rendering is naturally differentiable, the only input required to optimize the NeRF representation is a set of images with known camera poses.

The expected color C(r) of a camera ray r(t) = o + td with near and far bounds tn and tf is computed via the integral C(r) = ∫ from tn to tf of T(t)σ(r(t))c(r(t), d)dt, where T(t) = exp(−∫ from tn to t of σ(r(s))ds).
The volume density σ(x) can be interpreted as the differential probability of a ray terminating at an infinitesimal particle at location x.
The function T(t) denotes the accumulated transmittance along the ray from tn to t, i.e., the probability that the ray travels from tn to t without hitting any other particle.
The NeRF MLP FΘ first processes the input 3D coordinate x with 8 fully-connected layers (using ReLU activations and 256 channels per layer), and outputs σ and a 256-dimensional feature vector.

The 256-dimensional feature vector output by the initial 8 layers is concatenated with the camera ray's viewing direction and passed to one additional fully-connected layer (using a ReLU activation and 128 channels) that outputs the view-dependent RGB color.

The NeRF representation encourages multiview consistency by restricting the network to predict volume density σ as a function of only location x, while allowing RGB color c to be predicted as a function of both location and viewing direction.

The hierarchical volume sampling procedure simultaneously optimizes two networks: one "coarse" and one "fine", to increase rendering efficiency by allocating samples proportionally to their expected effect on the final rendering.
In hierarchical volume sampling, a set of Nc locations is first sampled using stratified sampling, and the "coarse" network is evaluated at these locations.
The alpha composited color from the coarse network Ĉc(r) is rewritten as a weighted sum of all sampled colors ci along the ray: Ĉc(r) = Σ from i=1 to Nc of wi ci, where wi = Ti(1 − exp(−σiδi)).
Normalizing the coarse network weights as ŵi = wi / Σ from j=1 to Nc of wj produces a piecewise-constant PDF along the ray.

A second set of Nf locations is sampled from the piecewise-constant PDF using inverse transform sampling, the "fine" network is evaluated at the union of the first and second set of samples, and the final rendered color of the ray Ĉf(r) is computed using all Nc+Nf samples.

Two improvements are introduced to enable NeRF to represent high-resolution complex scenes: a positional encoding of input coordinates that assists the MLP in representing high-frequency functions, and a hierarchical sampling procedure that allows efficient sampling of this high-frequency representation.
Having the network FΘ directly operate on xyzθφ input coordinates results in renderings that perform poorly at representing high-frequency variation in color and geometry.

The positional encoding function γ(p) = (sin(2^0 πp), cos(2^0 πp), ..., sin(2^{L-1} πp), cos(2^{L-1} πp)) is applied separately to each of the three coordinate values in x (normalized to lie in [−1, 1]) and to the three components of the Cartesian viewing direction unit vector d (which lie in [−1, 1]).
In NeRF experiments, L = 10 is used for the positional encoding of spatial coordinates γ(x) and L = 4 is used for the positional encoding of viewing directions γ(d).

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) rely upon specialized volumetric rendering algorithms based on ray marching that are mismatched to the capabilities of widely deployed graphics hardware.
MobileNeRF represents a NeRF as a set of polygons with textures representing binary opacities and feature vectors.

Traditional rendering of MobileNeRF polygons with a z-buffer yields an image with features at every pixel, which are interpreted by a small, view-dependent MLP running in a fragment shader to produce a final pixel color.

MobileNeRF enables NeRFs to be rendered with the traditional polygon rasterization pipeline, which provides massive pixel-level parallelism, achieving interactive frame rates on a wide range of compute platforms, including mobile phones.

Traditional NeRF implementations use a volumetric rendering algorithm that evaluates a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions along the ray for each pixel in order to estimate and integrate density and radiance.
The traditional NeRF volumetric rendering process is far too slow for interactive visualization.
SNeRG (Sparse Neural Radiance Grids) precomputation and deferred rendering approach increases the rendering speed of NeRF by three orders of magnitude.

SNeRG still relies upon ray marching through a sparse voxel grid to produce the features for each pixel, and thus it cannot fully utilize the parallelism available in commodity graphics processing units (GPUs).
SNeRG requires a significant amount of GPU memory to store the volumetric textures, which prohibits it from running on common mobile devices.
MobileNeRF's rendering pipeline does not sample rays or sort polygons in depth order, and thus can model only binary opacities.
MobileNeRF is 10× faster than SNeRG with the same output quality on standard test scenes.

fact_fields.method: MobileNeRF vs SNeRG rendering speed comparison

claim_records.text: MobileNeRF consumes less memory by storing surface textures instead of volumetric textures, enabling the method to run on integrated GPUs with limited memory and power.
MobileNeRF runs on a web browser and is compatible with all devices tested, as its viewer is an HTML webpage.
MobileNeRF allows real-time manipulation of reconstructed objects/scenes, as they are simple triangle meshes.
MobileNeRF does not need reconstructed 3D geometry as input.
Point-based representations for view synthesis often result in a lack of 3D consistency because their convolutional post-processing runs independently per output frame.
Point-based view synthesis representations require powerful desktop GPUs and have not been demonstrated to run on a mobile device.
DefTet differentiably renders a tetrahedral grid with occupancy and color at each vertex, then composites the interpolated values at all intersected faces along a ray.
NVDiffRec combines differentiable marching tetrahedra with differentiable rasterization to perform full inverse rendering and extract triangle meshes, materials, and lighting from images.
Differentiable inverse-rendering representations like DefTet and NVDiffRec incur a significant loss in view-synthesis quality.
While real-time rendering is possible with simple lighting for differentiable inverse-rendering representations, global illumination (GI) is computationally infeasible on mobile hardware.
MobileNeRF simply caches the outgoing radiance, which does not need expensive compute to model GI effects, and also results in higher view-synthesis quality.
Rendering a NeRF involves evaluating a large neural network at multiple 3D locations per pixel, preventing real-time rendering.

claim_records.text: Progressive Volume Distillation (PVD) is a systematic distillation method that enables any-to-any conversions between different NeRF architectures, including MLP, sparse or low-rank tensors, hashtables and their compositions.

PVD performs distillation progressively on different levels of volume representations from shallower to deeper, and employs special treatment of density to address its specific numerical instability problem.

With PVD, an MLP-based NeRF model distilled from a hashtable-based Instant-NGP model achieves a 10×~20× faster speed than training the original NeRF from scratch, while achieving a superior level of synthesis quality.
PVD is validated empirically on the NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF and TanksAndTemples datasets.
Hashtable-based NeRF representations admit faster training and rendering, but their lack of clear geometric meaning hampers downstream tasks like spatial-relation-aware editing.

In the Family and Barn scenes from the TanksAndTemples dataset, a NeRF model distilled by PVD from an INGP teacher within 1.5 hours achieves improved synthesis quality compared to a NeRF model trained from scratch using 25 hours.
PVD uses loss on intermediate volume representations (including output of φ1*, color and density) alongside the final rendered RGB volume to accelerate distillation.
PVD employs a special treatment of the dynamic density volume range by clipping, which improves training stability and significantly improves synthesis quality.
Distillation from hashtable and VM-decomposition structures often helps boost student model synthesis quality and consumes less time than training from scratch.
PVD builds a block-wise distillation strategy to accelerate the training procedure based on a unified view of different NeRF architectures.

NeRF architectures including plain MLP, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, hashtables and their compositions each have particular sets of trade-offs between training speed, rendering speed, and downstream task suitability.
PVD empowers downstream applications to optimally adapt neural NeRF representations for the task at hand in a post hoc fashion.

claim_records.text: NeRF generates a volumetric representation called a radiance field that creates color and density for every point within the relevant 3D space, rather than directly restoring the whole 3D scene geometry.
NeRF uses an interpolation approach to produce new 3D reconstructed views of complicated scenes.
CAMPARI simultaneously learns a camera generator and an image generator, enabling use of complex camera distributions without manual tuning.
CAMPARI represents scenes through foreground and background decomposition, leading to 3D-consistent representations and accurate camera distribution recovery.
CAMPARI surpasses baseline models that heavily depend on accurately matched camera distributions, due to its performance without camera parameter tuning.
Pix2NeRF introduces a pipeline to generate NeRF from a single input image, built upon π-GAN which maps latent codes to radiance fields.
Pix2NeRF employs an unsupervised approach and can be trained with independent images, with potential applications in 3D avatar generation, novel view synthesis, and super-resolution.
Pix2NeRF is currently restricted to work with only one category per dataset, impeding its ability to generalize to new categories.
Pix2NeRF is built on top of π-GAN but is not limited to using π-GAN as its backbone; newer generative NeRF models such as EG3D may achieve better visual quality if used as a backbone.

NeRF uses a deep neural network to represent complex scenes in a fully connected, non-convolutional way, with input as a continuous 5D coordinate and output as volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.
The 5D coordinate space for NeRF includes three dimensions for spatial coordinates (x,y,z) and two dimensions for camera viewing angles (θ,φ).
NeRF uses classic volume rendering techniques to synthesize views and is optimized using a set of images with known camera poses.
NeRF introduces a positional encoding and a hierarchical sampling strategy to address the inefficiency of the basic implementation.
Using input viewing direction, NeRF can represent non-Lambertian effects such as specularities.
NeRF uses a separate neural continuous volume representation network for each scene.
This survey categorizes and compares recent NeRF advances according to their architectural designs, especially in the field of novel view synthesis.

claim_records.text: Hyb-NeRF is a neural radiance field with a multi-resolution hybrid encoding that uses memory-efficient learnable positional features at coarse resolutions and hash-based feature grids at fine resolutions, achieving efficient neural modeling, fast rendering, and high-quality novel view synthesis.
Cone tracing-based features are embedded in the learnable positional encoding of Hyb-NeRF to eliminate encoding ambiguity and reduce aliasing artifacts.

fact_fields.method: cone tracing-based feature embedding in learnable positional encoding

claim_records.text: Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show Hyb-NeRF achieves faster rendering speed, better rendering quality, and lower memory footprint compared to previous state-of-the-art methods.
On the ficus scene in Blender, Hyb-NeRF with 16.4M parameters achieves 35.85 PSNR and 0.986 SSIM, compared to JNGP with 24.4M parameters achieving 33.23 PSNR and 0.981 SSIM.
All Hyb-NeRF models can reconstruct high-quality radiance fields in 9 minutes.

The smallest Hyb-NeRF model with 8.4M trainable parameters takes 4 minutes to achieve better rendering quality than state-of-the-art methods while requiring substantially less memory than previous and concurrent voxel-based methods.

Hyb-NeRF concatenates coarse-level learnable positional features with fine-level multi-resolution feature grids for multi-resolution scene representation, yielding detailed 3D reconstructions and high-quality rendering.
NeRF requires hundreds of network evaluations per pixel to approximate a volume rendering integral, making it slow to train.
Caching NeRFs into explicit data structures can effectively enhance rendering speed but at the cost of higher memory usage.

fact_fields.method: explicit data structure caching for NeRF

claim_records.text: Hash-based multi-resolution grid representation is fast to train and well suited to fast operation, but trainable features at coarse resolution levels have lower resolutions and are less compressed than feature grids at fine resolution levels, resulting in limited representation power and low memory efficiency.

claim_records.text: NeRF's rendering procedure samples a scene with a single ray per pixel and may produce renderings that are excessively blurred or aliased when training or testing images observe scene content at different resolutions.

The straightforward solution of supersampling by rendering with multiple rays per pixel is impractical for NeRF, because rendering each ray requires querying a multilayer perceptron hundreds of times.

fact_fields.method: supersampling with multiple rays per pixel

claim_records.text: mip-NeRF extends NeRF to represent the scene at a continuously-valued scale by efficiently rendering anti-aliased conical frustums instead of rays.
mip-NeRF reduces objectionable aliasing artifacts and significantly improves NeRF's ability to represent fine details, while also being 7% faster than NeRF and half the size.
Compared to NeRF, mip-NeRF reduces average error rates by 17% on the dataset presented with NeRF.
Compared to NeRF, mip-NeRF reduces average error rates by 60% on a challenging multiscale variant of the NeRF dataset.
Mip-NeRF is able to match the accuracy of a brute-force supersampled NeRF on the multiscale dataset while being 22x faster.

Mip-NeRF reasons about the 3D conical frustum defined by a camera pixel, and featurizes these conical frustums with integrated positional encoding (IPE) by approximating the frustum with a multivariate Gaussian and computing the closed-form integral E[γ(x)] over positional encodings of coordinates within the Gaussian.
When training images observe scene content at multiple resolutions, renderings from the recovered NeRF appear excessively blurred in close-up views and contain aliasing artifacts in distant views.

Mip-NeRF's scale-aware structure allows merging the separate 'coarse' and 'fine' MLPs used by NeRF for hierarchical sampling into a single MLP, making mip-NeRF slightly faster than NeRF (~7%) and having half as many parameters.
A NeRF trained on full-resolution images produces photorealistic renderings at new view locations only at the resolution or scale of the training images.
Adjusting camera intrinsics to reduce image resolution for a NeRF trained on full-resolution images results in renderings that exhibit severe aliasing.
Training a NeRF on multi-resolution images ameliorates aliasing issues slightly but results in poor quality renderings across scales: blur at full resolution, and 'jaggies' at low resolutions.
Mip-NeRF trained on multi-resolution images is capable of producing photorealistic renderings across different scales.

claim_records.text: Fourier PlenOctrees suffer from artifacts introduced by the involved compression when combined with recent state-of-the-art techniques for training static per-frame NeRF models.

The proposed novel density encoding adapts the Fourier-based compression to the characteristics of the transfer function used by the underlying volume rendering procedure and leads to a substantial reduction of artifacts in the dynamic model.

fact_fields.method: novel density encoding for Fourier PlenOctrees

claim_records.text: An augmentation of the training data is proposed that relaxes the periodicity assumption of the Fourier compression used in Fourier PlenOctrees.
PlenOctrees use a hierarchical octree structure of density and view-dependent radiance in terms of spherical harmonics (SH) to entirely avoid network evaluations.
Instant-NGP incorporated a multi-resolution hash encoding to significantly accelerate the training of neural models including NeRF.
Plenoxels stored SH and opacity values within a sparse voxel grid.
TensoRF factorized dense voxel grids into multiple low-rank components.

Fourier PlenOctrees (FPO) relaxed the limitation of ordinary PlenOctrees to only capture static scenes in a hierarchical manner by combining it with the Fourier transform which enables handling time-variant density and SH-based radiance in an efficient way.
During FPO construction, compression is performed on encoded densities σ′ = ecomp(elog(σ)), where the encoding consists of a component-dependent part and a logarithmic part.
The proposed encoding allows for a better reconstruction of the original densities without any fine-tuning than can be achieved with only the DFT and IDFT as proposed for FPOs.

fact_fields.method: proposed component-dependent + logarithmic density encoding vs DFT/IDFT-only FPO

claim_records.text: Non-negative density values σ are encoded logarithmically using elog(σ) = log(σ + 1) before applying the DFT, with the shift by 1 chosen so that elog remains a non-negative function for non-negative input densities with elog(0) = 0.
The logarithmic density encoding maps larger density values closer together while keeping smaller values almost unchanged, focusing approximation on densities near or equal to zero.
The encoded density sequences are easier to approximate with a low-frequency Fourier basis exploiting the properties of the transfer function.
The L2-error in fine-tuning is allowed to be larger for encoded high density values than without logarithmic encoding, focusing optimization on the more important parts of the reconstruction.
During rendering, the inverse of the logarithmic encoding elog(σ) = log(σ + 1) is applied after the IDFT to project densities back to their original range.

methods: novel density encoding for Fourier PlenOctrees
proposed component-dependent + logarithmic density encoding vs DFT/IDFT-only FPO

claim_records.text: Existing 3D reconstruction methods including NeRF require excessive runtime for rendering, making them impractical for daily applications.
EvaSurf first employs an efficient surface-based model with a multi-view supervision module to ensure accurate mesh reconstruction.
EvaSurf learns an implicit texture embedded with a set of Gaussian lobes to capture view-dependent information for high-fidelity rendering.
EvaSurf employs a lightweight neural shader with explicit geometry and implicit texture to reduce computation expense and support real-time rendering on common mobile devices.
EvaSurf can reconstruct high-quality appearance and accurate mesh on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
EvaSurf can be trained in just 1-2 hours using a single GPU.
EvaSurf can run on mobile devices at over 40 FPS (Frames Per Second).
The final package required for EvaSurf rendering takes up only 40-50 MB.

claim_records.text: The rendering scheme in neural radiance field (NeRF) is effective in rendering a pixel by casting a ray into the scene.
NeRF yields blurred rendering results when the training images are captured at non-uniform scales.
NeRF produces aliasing artifacts if the test images are taken in distant views.
Mip-NeRF proposes a multiscale representation as a conical frustum to encode scale information.
Mip-NeRF is only suitable for offline rendering since it relies on integrated positional encoding (IPE) to query a multilayer perceptron (MLP).
Mip-VoG is an explicit multiscale representation with a deferred architecture for real-time anti-aliasing rendering.
Mip-VoG includes a density Mip-VoG for scene geometry and a feature Mip-VoG with a small MLP for view-dependent color.
Mip-VoG encodes scene scale using the level of detail (LOD) derived from ray differentials.
Mip-VoG uses quadrilinear interpolation to map a queried 3D location to its features and density from two neighboring downsampled voxel grids.
Mip-VoG is the first approach to offer multiscale training and real-time anti-aliasing rendering simultaneously.
Experiments on multiscale datasets show that Mip-VoG outperforms state-of-the-art real-time rendering baselines.

pixelNeRF introduces an architecture that conditions a NeRF on image inputs in a fully convolutional manner.

claim_records.text: CLIP-NeRF is a multi-modal 3D object manipulation method for neural radiance fields that leverages the joint language-image embedding space of the CLIP model.
CLIP-NeRF allows manipulating NeRF using either a short text prompt or an exemplar image.
CLIP-NeRF introduces a disentangled conditional NeRF architecture that allows individual control over both shape and appearance.
In CLIP-NeRF, shape conditioning is achieved by applying a learned deformation field to the positional encoding, and color conditioning is deferred to the volumetric rendering stage.
CLIP-NeRF designs two code mappers that take a CLIP embedding as input and update the latent codes to reflect the targeted editing.
The CLIP-NeRF code mappers are trained with a CLIP-based matching loss to ensure manipulation accuracy.

claim_records.text: NeRF trains a deep network to map 5D input coordinates representing spatial location and viewing direction into a volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance.
NeRF is only applicable to static scenes where the same spatial location can be queried from different images.

D-NeRF extends neural radiance fields to a dynamic domain, allowing reconstruction and rendering of novel images of objects under rigid and non-rigid motions from a single camera moving around the scene.

D-NeRF treats time as an additional input and splits learning into two stages: one encoding the scene into a canonical space, and another mapping the canonical representation into the deformed scene at a particular time.
Both mappings in D-NeRF are simultaneously learned using fully-connected networks.
After training, D-NeRF can render novel images while controlling both the camera view and the time variable, and thus the object movement.
D-NeRF demonstrates effectiveness on scenes with objects under rigid, articulated and non-rigid motions.

claim_records.text: NeRF has emerged as a powerful representation for novel view synthesis due to its simplicity and state-of-the-art performance.
NeRF can produce photorealistic renderings of unseen viewpoints when many input views are available.
NeRF performance drops significantly when the number of input views is reduced.
The majority of artifacts in sparse input NeRF scenarios are caused by errors in estimated scene geometry and by divergent behavior at the start of training.
RegNeRF regularizes the geometry and appearance of patches rendered from unobserved viewpoints, and anneals the ray sampling space during training.
RegNeRF additionally uses a normalizing flow model to regularize the color of unobserved viewpoints.
RegNeRF outperforms other methods that optimize over a single scene.
In many cases, RegNeRF also outperforms conditional models that are extensively pre-trained on large multi-view datasets.

claim_records.text: NeRF and its variants require a lengthy training time ranging from hours to days for reconstructing a single scene.
The proposed direct voxel grid optimization approach achieves NeRF-comparable quality and converges from scratch in less than 15 minutes with a single GPU.
The proposed representation uses a density voxel grid for scene geometry and a feature voxel grid with a shallow network for complex view-dependent appearance.
Post-activation interpolation on voxel density is capable of producing sharp surfaces in lower grid resolution.
Imposing several priors robustifies the direct voxel density optimization process, which is otherwise prone to suboptimal geometry solutions.

fact_fields.method: Imposing several priors on direct voxel density optimization

claim_records.text: Evaluation on five inward-facing benchmarks shows the proposed method matches, if not surpasses, NeRF's quality while taking about 15 minutes to train from scratch for a new scene.

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) have low rendering efficiency due to the need for multiple network forwardings to render a single pixel.
Existing Neural Light Field (NeLF) methods require significantly larger network capacities to achieve visual quality close to NeRF, which limits their rendering efficiency in practice.
The proposed Neural Radiance Distribution Field (NeRDF) uses a small network similar to NeRF while preserving rendering speed with a single network forwarding per pixel as in NeLF.
The proposed NeRDF method achieves a ~254x speed-up over NeRF with similar network size, with only a marginal performance decline.
The proposed NeRDF method offers a better trade-off among speed, quality, and network size than existing methods.

claim_records.text: VQ-NeRF reduces the sampling space of NeRF to a lower resolution and reinstates it to the original size using a pre-trained VAE decoder to mitigate the sampling time bottleneck during rendering.
VQ-NeRF uses a multi-scale NeRF sampling scheme that concurrently optimizes the NeRF model at both compressed and original scales to enhance the network's ability to preserve fine details.
VQ-NeRF incorporates a semantic loss function to improve the geometric fidelity and semantic coherence of 3D reconstructions.
Evaluation on the DTU, BlendMVS, and H3DS datasets confirms the superior performance of the VQ-NeRF approach.
VQ-NeRF achieves the optimal trade-off between rendering quality and efficiency.

claim_records.text: The introduced 3D Hierarchical Proxy Node representation represents an object's shape and texture via a sparse set of hierarchically organized (tree-structured) proxy nodes distributed on its surface and interior, with each node storing local shape and texture information implicitly encoded by a small MLP within its neighborhood.
Querying any 3D coordinate's properties in the Hierarchical Proxy Node framework involves efficient neural interpolation and lightweight decoding from relevant nearby and parent nodes.

The Hierarchical Proxy Node framework yields a highly compact representation where nodes align with local semantics, enabling direct drag-and-edit manipulation and offering scalable quality-complexity control.
Extensive experiments across 3D reconstruction and editing demonstrate the HPR3D method's expressive efficiency, high-fidelity rendering quality, and superior editability.

Current 3D representations including meshes, voxels, point clouds, and NeRF-based neural implicit fields are often task-specific, lacking universal applicability across reconstruction, generation, editing, and driving.
NeRFs deliver excellent rendering but suffer from structural ambiguity, hindering animation and manipulation.
Meshes offer high precision but their dense vertex data complicates editing.

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) typically struggle to reconstruct and render highly specular objects, whose appearance varies quickly with changes in viewpoint.
Recent NeRF works have improved ability to render detailed specular appearance of distant environment illumination, but are unable to synthesize consistent reflections of closer content.

fact_fields.method: recent NeRF-based specular appearance modeling approaches

claim_records.text: These recent specular NeRF techniques rely on large computationally-expensive neural networks to model outgoing radiance, which severely limits optimization and rendering speed.

The proposed NeRF-Casting approach casts reflection rays from points along each camera ray and traces them through the NeRF representation to render feature vectors which are decoded into color using a small inexpensive network, instead of querying an expensive neural network for outgoing view-dependent radiance at those points.
The NeRF-Casting model outperforms prior methods for view synthesis of scenes containing shiny objects.
NeRF-Casting is the only existing NeRF method that can synthesize photorealistic specular appearance and reflections in real-world scenes.
NeRF-Casting requires comparable optimization time to current state-of-the-art view synthesis models.

claim_records.text: Rendering a single pixel in NeRF requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times.
Rendering a pixel in NeLF amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching.
The proposed method uses a deep residual MLP network with 88 layers to effectively learn the light field.
The key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which knowledge is transferred from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation.
On synthetic scenes, the proposed method achieves 26-35x FLOPs reduction per camera ray compared to NeRF.
On synthetic scenes, the proposed method achieves 28-31x runtime speedup compared to NeRF.
On synthetic scenes, the proposed method delivers 1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement over NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

claim_records.text: The proposed LLNeRF approach enhances the scene representation and synthesizes normal-light novel views directly from sRGB low-light images in an unsupervised manner.

Experiments demonstrate that LLNeRF outperforms existing low-light enhancement methods and NeRF methods.

claim_records.text: Original NeRF requires querying a deep Multi-Layer Perceptron millions of times, leading to slow rendering times even on modern GPUs.
Real-time rendering is possible by utilizing thousands of tiny MLPs instead of one single large MLP, where each individual MLP only represents parts of the scene.

Combining the divide-and-conquer tiny MLP strategy with further optimizations accelerates rendering by three orders of magnitude compared to the original NeRF model without incurring high storage costs.

fact_fields.method: KiloNeRF with divide-and-conquer tiny MLP strategy plus further optimizations

claim_records.text: Using teacher-student distillation for training, the KiloNeRF speed-up can be achieved without sacrificing visual quality.
NeRF synthesizes novel views of a scene with unprecedented quality by fitting a neural radiance field to RGB images.

claim_records.text: Existing Human NeRF methods for reconstructing 3D humans typically rely on multiple 2D images from multi-view cameras or monocular videos captured from fixed camera views.
Human images captured from random camera angles present challenges for high-quality 3D human reconstruction.
SHERF is the first generalizable Human NeRF model for recovering animatable 3D humans from a single input image.
SHERF extracts and encodes 3D human representations in canonical space, enabling rendering and animation from free views and poses.
SHERF uses a bank of 3D-aware hierarchical features including global, point-level, and pixel-aligned features to facilitate informative encoding of 3D human representations.
SHERF uses a feature fusion transformer to effectively integrate the 3D-aware hierarchical feature bank.

Extensive experiments on THuman, RenderPeople, ZJU_MoCap, and HuMMan datasets demonstrate that SHERF achieves state-of-the-art performance, with better generalizability for novel view and pose synthesis.

claim_records.text: On the algorithm level, RT-NeRF integrates an efficient rendering pipeline that directly computes the geometry of pre-existing points to largely alleviate inefficiency caused by the commonly adopted uniform point sampling method in NeRF.
RT-NeRF leverages a coarse-grained view-dependent computing ordering scheme to eliminate unnecessary processing of invisible points.

The RT-NeRF hardware accelerator adopts a hybrid encoding scheme that adaptively switches between bitmap- or coordinate-based sparsity encoding formats for NeRF's sparse embeddings, to maximize storage savings and reduce required DRAM accesses while supporting efficient NeRF decoding.

claim_records.text: The RT-NeRF hardware accelerator integrates both a dual-purpose bi-direction adder & search tree and a high-density sparse search unit to coordinate the two supported sparsity encoding formats.

claim_records.text: Most current NeRF methods require intensive resources due to ray marching-based rendering.

The Deformable Neural Mesh Primitive (DNMP) is a flexible and compact neural variant of classic mesh representation, consisting of a set of connected deformable mesh vertices with paired vertex features to parameterize the geometry and radiance information of a local area.
DNMP enforces the shape of each primitive to be decoded from a relatively low-dimensional latent space to constrain the degree of freedom for optimization and lower storage budgets.
DNMP decodes rendering colors from vertex features (interpolated with rasterization) by a view-dependent MLP.

fact_fields.method: rasterization-interpolated vertex feature decoding via view-dependent MLP

claim_records.text: The DNMP method achieves leading performance for novel view synthesis in urban scenarios.
The DNMP representation enables fast rendering at 2.07ms per 1k pixels and low peak memory usage of 110MB per 1k pixels.
The lightweight version of DNMP can run 33 times faster than vanilla NeRFs, with a rendering speed of 0.61ms per 1k pixels, comparable to the highly-optimized Instant-NGP's 0.71ms per 1k pixels.

claim_records.text: Existing NeRF-like models often produce blurry or low-resolution renderings in unbounded scenes due to the unbalanced detail and scale of nearby and distant objects.
Existing NeRF-like models are slow to train in unbounded scene settings.
Existing NeRF-like models may exhibit artifacts in unbounded scenes due to the inherent ambiguity of reconstructing a large scene from a small set of images.
The mip-NeRF 360 model uses a non-linear scene parameterization, online distillation, and a novel distortion-based regularizer to address unbounded scene challenges as an extension of mip-NeRF.
mip-NeRF 360 reduces mean-squared error by 57% compared to mip-NeRF on targeted scenes where the camera rotates 360 degrees around a point.
mip-NeRF 360 is able to produce realistic synthesized views and detailed depth maps for highly intricate, unbounded real-world scenes.

claim_records.text: The presented method synthesizes novel views of complex scenes by interpolating a sparse set of nearby views.

The core network architecture of the method includes a multilayer perceptron and a ray transformer that estimates radiance and volume density at continuous 5D locations (3D spatial locations and 2D viewing directions).
The method draws appearance information on the fly from multiple source views at render time.
Drawing on source views at render time allows the method to render high-resolution imagery.
Unlike neural scene representation work that optimizes per-scene functions for rendering, the method learns a generic view interpolation function that generalizes to novel scenes.
The method renders images using classic volume rendering, which is fully differentiable and allows training using only multi-view posed images as supervision.
Experiments show that the method outperforms recent novel view synthesis methods that also seek to generalize to novel scenes.
If fine-tuned on each scene, the method is competitive with state-of-the-art single-scene neural rendering methods.

claim_records.text: 3DGS is introduced into indoor 3D Object Detection for the first time in this work.
3DGS primarily relies on 2D pixel-level supervision, resulting in unclear 3D spatial distribution of Gaussian blobs and poor differentiation between objects and background, which hinders indoor 3DOD.
2D images typically include numerous background pixels, leading to densely reconstructed 3DGS with many noisy Gaussian blobs representing the background, negatively affecting detection.
Incorporating 2D Boundary Guidance significantly enhances the spatial distribution of Gaussian blobs, resulting in clearer differentiation between objects and their background.

The proposed Box-Focused Sampling strategy uses 2D boxes to generate object probability distribution in 3D space, allowing effective probabilistic sampling in 3D to retain more object blobs and reduce noisy background blobs.
3DGS-DET achieves an improvement of +6.0 on mAP@0.25 over NeRF-Det++ on the ScanNet dataset.
3DGS-DET achieves an improvement of +7.8 on mAP@0.5 over NeRF-Det++ on the ScanNet dataset.
3DGS-DET achieves an improvement of +14.9 on mAP@0.25 over NeRF-Det++ on the ARKITScenes dataset.
NeRF has been adapted for indoor 3D Object Detection via view-synthesis representation, but its implicit nature limits representational capacity.

claim_records.text: VDN-NeRF is a method to train neural radiance fields for better geometry under non-Lambertian surface and dynamic lighting conditions that cause significant variation in the radiance of a point when viewed from different angles.

VDN-NeRF normalizes view-dependence by distilling invariant information already encoded in the learned NeRFs, rather than explicitly modeling the underlying factors that result in the view-dependent phenomenon.
VDN-NeRF jointly trains NeRFs for view synthesis with view-dependence normalization to attain quality geometry.

Experiments show that even though shape-radiance ambiguity is inevitable, the proposed normalization can minimize its effect on geometry, which essentially aligns the optimal capacity needed for explaining view-dependent variations.
VDN-NeRF applies to various baselines and significantly improves geometry without changing the volume rendering pipeline, even if the data is captured under a moving light source.

claim_records.text: Neural approaches such as NeRF have achieved remarkable success in view synthesis, but do not explicitly perform decomposition and instead operate exclusively on radiance, the product of reflectance and illumination.
Extensions to NeRF, such as NeRD, can perform decomposition but struggle to accurately recover detailed illumination, thereby significantly limiting realism.
The proposed reflectance decomposition network can estimate shape, BRDF, and per-image illumination given a set of object images captured under varying illumination.
Neural-PIL is a novel illumination integration network that replaces a costly illumination integral operation in the rendering with a simple network query.
Deep low-dimensional priors on BRDF and illumination representations are learned using novel smooth manifold auto-encoders.
The decompositions can result in considerably better BRDF and light estimates enabling more accurate novel view-synthesis and relighting compared to prior art.

claim_records.text: NeuDA is a flexible neural implicit representation leveraging hierarchical voxel grids for high-fidelity surface reconstruction.
Each vertex in NeuDA's hierarchical anchor grids stores a 3D position (anchor) instead of a direct embedding (feature).
Optimizing NeuDA's anchor grids allows different local geometry structures to be adaptively encoded.
NeuDA introduces a simple hierarchical positional encoding method for the hierarchical anchor structure to flexibly exploit properties of high-frequency and low-frequency geometry and appearance.
Experiments on both the DTU and BlendedMVS datasets demonstrate that NeuDA can produce promising mesh surfaces.

Previous differentiable ray casting works IDR and NeuS overlook spatial context in 3D space when predicting and rendering surfaces, and may fail to capture sharp local topologies such as small holes and structures.

claim_records.text: HollowNeRF delivers comparable rendering quality to Instant-NGP while utilizing just 31% of the parameters.
HollowNeRF can achieve a PSNR accuracy gain of up to 1dB using only 56% of the parameters.

HollowNeRF trains a coarse 3D saliency mask that guides efficient feature pruning, and employs an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) pruner to sparsify the 3D saliency mask during training.
HollowNeRF exploits sparsity in the 3D scene to redistribute hash collisions, improving rendering quality while using a fraction of the parameters of comparable state-of-the-art solutions.
