claim_records.text: Prior radiance field methods achieving high visual quality require neural networks that are costly to train and render.
Recent faster radiance field methods inevitably trade off speed for quality.
For unbounded and complete scenes rather than isolated objects at 1080p resolution rendering, no current method can achieve real-time display rates.
The introduced 3D Gaussian splatting method achieves state-of-the-art visual quality while maintaining competitive training times and high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis at 1080p resolution.
The introduced method represents scenes with 3D Gaussians starting from sparse points produced during camera calibration.
The introduced method performs interleaved optimization and density control of 3D Gaussians, notably optimizing anisotropic covariance to achieve an accurate representation of the scene.
The introduced method develops a fast visibility-aware rendering algorithm that supports anisotropic splatting and both accelerates training and allows real-time rendering.
The introduced method achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and real-time rendering on several established datasets.

claim_records.text: OReX is a method for 3D shape reconstruction from slices alone, featuring a Neural Field as the interpolation prior.
A modest neural network trained on input planes returns an inside/outside estimate for a given 3D coordinate, yielding a prior that induces smoothness and self-similarities.

OReX uses an iterative estimation architecture and a hierarchical input sampling scheme that encourage coarse-to-fine training, allowing the training process to focus on high frequencies at later stages.

fact_fields.method: iterative estimation architecture and hierarchical input sampling scheme

claim_records.text: OReX mitigates a ripple-like effect stemming from the mesh extraction step by regularizing the spatial gradients of the indicator function around input in/out boundaries during network training.

fact_fields.method: regularizing spatial gradients of the indicator function around input in/out boundaries during network training

claim_records.text: Through extensive qualitative and quantitative experimentation, OReX is demonstrated to be robust, accurate, and scales well with the size of the input.
OReX reports state-of-the-art results compared to previous approaches and recent potential solutions.

assertions.source_quote: Foundational NeRF represents one scene as a continuous coordinate-based MLP field mapping 3D position and viewing direction to emitted RGB color and volume density. Density depends on position alone, supporting view-consistent occupancy and occlusion, while color may depend on viewing direction to represent view-dependent appearance. Camera rays are evaluated at sampled points, and differentiable emission-absorption volume rendering composites local colors using interval opacity and accumulated transmittance. Photometric loss between rendered and observed pixels, with known poses, back-propagates through this quadrature to optimize the MLP. Positional encoding and coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling are practical components that improve high-frequency detail and allocate more samples to contributing ray segments, but the baseline remains a per-scene continuous neural field rather than an explicit mesh, voxel model, or feed-forward reconstructor. assertions.source_quote: At the representation level, NeRF defines a scene as a continuous 5D vector-valued function. Its input is a 3D spatial location x=(x,y,z) and a viewing direction, written in the original paper as (θ,φ) and implemented as a 3D Cartesian unit vector d; its output is an emitted RGB color c=(r,g,b) and a volume density σ. A multilayer perceptron FΘ approximates the mapping (x,d)→(c,σ), with separate treatment of geometry and appearance: density is predicted from position alone, while color may depend on both position and viewing direction. This design encourages multiview-consistent occupancy while allowing view-dependent appearance such as specular effects. assertions.source_quote: For rendering, NeRF casts a camera ray r(t)=o+td and evaluates the network at sample locations along that ray. Classical volume rendering accumulates the samples into a pixel color: each sample contributes its color weighted by its local opacity, (1−exp(−σ_iδ_i)), and by accumulated transmittance T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jδ_j), where δ_i is the distance between adjacent samples. The resulting discrete sum is Ĉ(r)=Σ_i T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i))c_i, with a background term when ray termination is modeled. This quadrature is a piecewise-constant approximation to the continuous emission-absorption integral and is differentiable, so gradients from rendered pixels can update the MLP weights. assertions.source_quote: Training therefore requires only images and known camera poses in the original setup: NeRF renders rays from the training viewpoints, compares predicted colors with observed pixel colors, and back-propagates the rendering loss through the compositing and network evaluations. The original method also uses positional encoding to expose high-frequency coordinate variation and a coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling strategy: a coarse network estimates sample weights, and a fine network receives additional samples drawn from the normalized coarse weights so that more evaluations concentrate where the ray is expected to contribute. These components make the foundational model a per-scene optimized continuous field, not a generic mesh or an explicit voxel reconstruction. assertions.source_quote: For this review, the organizing choice is a pipeline-based grouping: representation, rendering operator, and optimization objective. This grouping is used to explain the foundational NeRF formulation; it is not a universal taxonomy of all neural-rendering methods, nor is it a paper-proposed classification. Under this grouping, the defining relationship is that a continuous field supplies density and color at queried coordinates, differentiable volume rendering composites those samples along camera rays, and the resulting pixel error supervises the field. Later methods can still be NeRF-like if they preserve this field-to-ray-compositing relationship, even when they change the data structure or sampling strategy. assertions.source_quote: The first classification criterion is what represents the scene. The original NeRF uses a per-scene, coordinate-based MLP: the network parameters encode a continuous function over 3D position and viewing direction rather than storing colors on an explicit mesh or a fixed voxel grid. This separates it from representations whose primary scene store is polygons, textured meshes, voxel textures, hash tables, sparse tensors, or other explicit feature structures. Such structures may be used to accelerate, bake, distill, or rasterize a NeRF-derived model, but they are different implementation choices from the original continuous MLP field. assertions.source_quote: The second criterion is how geometry and appearance are factorized within the representation. In foundational NeRF, density is constrained to be a function of position only, whereas emitted RGB color can depend on position and viewing direction. That distinction is important: density supplies the view-invariant occupancy used by transmittance and occlusion, while directional color permits non-Lambertian or specular appearance. Methods that replace the view-dependent color shader with diffuse texture plus residuals, surface texture plus view-aware lobes, reflection-ray tracing, or learned feature decoding alter the appearance model; they should not be read as changing the original density-color distinction by itself. assertions.source_quote: The third criterion is the rendering integral and its discretization. Foundational NeRF casts one ray through each pixel, queries the field at points along that ray, and alpha-composites colors using local opacity and accumulated transmittance. This is emission-absorption volume rendering, not direct z-buffered surface rendering. A method that rasterizes textured polygons or mesh primitives and then invokes a small shader changes the primary visibility mechanism, even if it retains view-dependent color or was trained from a NeRF. Conversely, mip-NeRF remains closely related to the original ray-based formulation but replaces infinitesimal ray samples with anti-aliased conical frustums to encode scale, addressing blur and aliasing rather than replacing volume compositing with rasterization. This is emission-absorption volume rendering, not direct z-buffered surface rendering. A method that rasterizes textured polygons or mesh primitives and then invokes a small shader changes the primary visibility mechanism, even if it retains view-dependent color or was trained from a NeRF. Conversely, mip-NeRF remains closely related to the original ray-based formulation but replaces infinitesimal ray samples with anti-aliased conical frustums to encode scale, addressing blur and aliasing rather than replacing volume compositing with rasterization. assertions.source_quote: The fourth criterion is sampling scope. Hierarchical volume sampling in the original NeRF is an efficiency allocation mechanism inside the same rendering formulation: a coarse network evaluates stratified samples, its normalized compositing weights define a piecewise-constant distribution, and inverse-transform sampling adds fine samples in regions expected to affect the pixel. The fine result still uses volume rendering over the union of samples. This differs from deployment-oriented acceleration schemes that bake the field, use deferred shaders, rasterize polygons, employ explicit level-of-detail structures, or partition large scenes; those change storage, hardware use, or visibility computation, whereas coarse-to-fine sampling changes where the MLP is queried. assertions.source_quote: The final criterion is supervision and applicability. The original setup optimizes one scene from multiple posed images by comparing rendered and observed colors; it does not require explicit 3D labels in that formulation. Feed-forward or conditional NeRFs, single-image reconstruction systems, and generative diffusion-coupled methods introduce learned priors or additional conditioning and therefore solve a different data-regime problem from the original per-scene optimization. Likewise, methods focused on multiscale anti-aliasing, mobile frame rate, urban scale, geometry extraction, editing, or architecture conversion are related along selected pipeline dimensions but have distinct objectives; their results cannot be treated as direct rankings unless datasets, hardware, training views, and metrics are matched. assertions.source_quote: Geometry and appearance are deliberately factorized inside the MLP. Density is restricted to depend only on 3D position x, so the same spatial location has one occupancy field across viewpoints. Color is allowed to depend on both x and viewing direction d, which gives the model a mechanism for view-dependent non-Lambertian appearance such as specular highlights. In the original architecture, eight fully connected ReLU layers with 256 channels process position and output σ plus a 256-dimensional feature; that feature is concatenated with the ray direction and passed through an additional fully connected ReLU layer with 128 channels to predict RGB. assertions.source_quote: A camera ray is written as r(t)=o+td, with origin o and unit direction d. NeRF evaluates the field at coordinates sampled along this ray and turns those local field values into one pixel color. This makes the representation volumetric: visibility is not decided by intersecting a single surface, but by accumulating emission and occlusion through the density distribution along the ray. The same ray-sampling procedure is used during training and novel-view rendering; only the camera pose and image pixels change. This makes the representation volumetric: visibility is not decided by intersecting a single surface, but by accumulating emission and occlusion through the density distribution along the ray. The same ray-sampling procedure is used during training and novel-view rendering; only the camera pose and image pixels change. assertions.source_quote: The continuous physical model is an emission-absorption volume integral. For a ray r(t), color is C(r)=∫ c(r(t),d) σ(r(t)) T(t) dt, where T(t)=exp(−∫_0^t σ(r(s))ds) is accumulated transmittance: the probability that light traveling from distance t toward the camera has not been stopped by earlier density. In this formulation, σ acts as an absorption coefficient or density field, while c is the radiance emitted at that location toward direction d. A finite far-boundary term can account for light entering from the background. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:bb48bf662d06] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:8ad33082e01a]

assertions.source_quote: NeRF approximates the integral numerically at N samples along each ray. If t_i is a sample, δ_i is the interval width to the next sample, σ_i and c_i are the network outputs at that sample, and T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jδ_j), then the discrete alpha-composited color is Ĉ(r)=Σ_{i=1}^{N} T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i))c_i, plus the background contribution weighted by remaining transmittance where used. The factor α_i=1−exp(−σ_iδ_i) is the local opacity assigned to the interval, while T_i is the product of earlier interval transmittances. This quadrature treats the field as approximately constant over each sampled neighborhood. assertions.source_quote: Differentiability is the key property that connects rendering to representation learning. The sampled colors, densities, interval widths, transmittance products, and final pixel color form a computation graph through which a photometric rendering loss can be back-propagated to the MLP parameters. The original optimization compares colors rendered from training camera rays with observed ground-truth pixel colors; no explicit 3D geometry labels are required by this basic formulation. In other words, multi-view image consistency, mediated by known camera poses, supervises the continuous density and radiance function. assertions.source_quote: Naive dense quadrature is expensive because the network is evaluated at many points along every pixel ray, including empty space and regions hidden behind visible content. Foundational NeRF therefore uses hierarchical volume sampling with two networks, called coarse and fine. The coarse network first evaluates N_c stratified samples along a ray. Its rendered color is rewritten as a weighted sum, with sample weights w_i=T_i(1−exp(−σ_iδ_i)); after normalization, these weights define a piecewise-constant probability distribution over ray segments. assertions.source_quote: The applicability boundary of foundational NeRF is narrower than that of the broader NeRF family. It optimizes a separate network for each scene, requires training images with known camera poses in the original setup, and renders by querying an MLP many times per ray. Consequently, later methods that condition a NeRF on input images, distill between MLP and explicit-grid architectures, bake features into voxels, rasterize polygons, trace reflection rays, or model surfaces and textures are modifying the data regime, representation store, rendering path, or appearance model; they should not be described as merely repeating the original 5D MLP and ray-marching mechanism. assertions.source_quote: Two later comparisons clarify what is and is not changed in the foundational formulation. Mip-NeRF retains the neural-field and anti-aliased volume-rendering lineage but queries conical frustums with integrated positional encoding so that scale-dependent blur and aliasing can be modeled; it targets a sampling limitation of one ray per pixel. MobileNeRF instead changes deployment-oriented visibility by representing a baked NeRF with textured polygons and using z-buffer rasterization followed by a small view-dependent MLP. These are related NeRF-derived systems, but neither is the same mechanism as the original continuous MLP evaluated at point samples along camera rays. assertions.source_quote: The discrete rendering experiment also exposes the main cost dimension. Each pixel requires a camera ray, and each ray requires many MLP evaluations at sample positions; dense quadrature repeatedly queries free space and occluded regions that contribute little or nothing to the final color. Hierarchical sampling mitigates this waste inside NeRF by biasing later samples toward expected content, but it does not change the fundamental requirement of network evaluation along rays. Consequently, the original method's evidence supports high-quality offline view synthesis more directly than interactive rendering; later speed claims must be attributed to their changed representations or rendering pipelines. assertions.source_quote: Mip-NeRF is the closest selected comparison on the rendering-sampling dimension because it preserves the neural radiance-field lineage but changes the query primitive from an infinitesimal point sample along a single ray to an anti-aliased conical frustum encoding continuous scale. On the dataset presented with NeRF, mip-NeRF is reported to reduce average error rates by 17% relative to NeRF; on a challenging multiscale variant introduced by mip-NeRF, the reduction is 60%. It is also reported to be about 7% faster than NeRF, half the size, and capable of matching brute-force supersampled NeRF accuracy on the multiscale dataset while being 22× faster. These results are specific to the scale/anti-aliasing setting and should not be generalized as ordinary fixed-resolution superiority. assertions.source_quote: Mip-NeRF is the closest selected comparison on the rendering-sampling dimension because it preserves the neural radiance-field lineage but changes the query primitive from an infinitesimal point sample along a single ray to an anti-aliased conical frustum encoding continuous scale. On the dataset presented with NeRF, mip-NeRF is reported to reduce average error rates by 17% relative to NeRF; on a challenging multiscale variant introduced by mip-NeRF, the reduction is 60%. It is also reported to be about 7% faster than NeRF, half the size, and capable of matching brute-force supersampled NeRF accuracy on the multiscale dataset while being 22× faster. These results are specific to the scale/anti-aliasing setting and should not be generalized as ordinary fixed-resolution superiority. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:4e785aa745fe] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:b14753cf9c18] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:section:abstract:3:97643459cce9:claim:4cdea39204ef]
assertions.claim_text: The mip-NeRF results should not be generalized as ordinary fixed-resolution superiority.

assertions.source_quote: The mip-NeRF comparison also clarifies why supersampling is not an apples-to-apples baseline for interactive use. Casting multiple rays per pixel can reduce aliasing, but runtime generally scales with the supersampling rate because every extra ray still requires hundreds of MLP queries in NeRF. Mip-NeRF's reported 22× speed advantage is relative to brute-force supersampled NeRF on the authors' multiscale dataset, not relative to every explicit-grid or rasterization accelerator. Likewise, its 7% speed gain over NeRF and half-as-large model arise from integrating coarse and fine sampling into a single MLP in that system; they are not properties of the original coarse-plus-fine NeRF architecture. assertions.source_quote: A later multiscale system, Mip-VoG, addresses a different deployment point from mip-NeRF. It uses explicit multiscale mip voxel grids, ray-differential level-of-detail, quadrilinear interpolation across neighboring downsampled grids, a density grid, and a feature grid with a small MLP for view-dependent color. The authors state that mip-NeRF relies on integrated positional encoding and MLP queries and is therefore suited to offline rendering, whereas Mip-VoG targets simultaneous multiscale training and real-time anti-aliased rendering. Their reported result is superiority over state-of-the-art real-time rendering baselines on multiscale datasets; the supplied excerpt does not provide matched metric values or a direct head-to-head runtime table against original NeRF, so no numerical ranking can be reconstructed here. assertions.source_quote: Deployment-oriented methods change the primary visibility mechanism and therefore do not yield a like-for-like NeRF rendering-quality score. MobileNeRF represents a baked NeRF as textured polygons carrying binary opacities and feature vectors; z-buffer rasterization produces per-pixel features, and a small view-dependent MLP in a fragment shader decodes the final color. Its evidence targets interactive frame rates across commodity platforms, including mobile devices, by exploiting standard polygon rasterization rather than specialized ray marching. This comparison supports a hardware-pipeline and latency objective, but the selected excerpt does not supply a common dataset metric table against the original NeRF implementation. assertions.source_quote: SNeRG illustrates the same distinction one step before MobileNeRF. It bakes NeRF into a sparse neural radiance grid in which active voxels store opacity, diffuse color, and a learned feature vector; ray marching first accumulates diffuse colors and features, and a lightweight deferred MLP converts the accumulated feature into a view-dependent residual. The source reports that this precomputation and deferred rendering increase NeRF rendering speed by three orders of magnitude, but also notes continued dependence on ray marching through a sparse voxel grid and substantial GPU memory for volumetric textures. Thus, the speed result is tied to baking and altered storage, not to the original MLP-only representation, and it comes with a memory trade-off. assertions.source_quote: Architecture-conversion evidence is also distinct from view-synthesis benchmarking. PVD converts among MLP, sparse-tensor, low-rank-tensor, hash-table, and composite NeRF representations through progressive volume distillation, with special density handling for numerical stability. On NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF, and TanksAndTemples, the authors report that an MLP-based NeRF student distilled from a hash-table-based Instant-NGP teacher can be trained 10× to 20× faster than training the original NeRF from scratch while attaining superior synthesis quality. That comparison concerns post hoc representation conversion and training cost under PVD's distillation protocol; it does not show that an ordinary from-scratch MLP NeRF is intrinsically 10–20× slower than every other method or that quality is identical across all architecture pairs. assertions.source_quote: The main computational limitation follows directly from the foundational rendering equation. NeRF must cast a ray for each pixel and evaluate an MLP at hundreds of sample positions along that ray to estimate and integrate density and radiance; free space and occluded regions can still be queried repeatedly. Coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling allocates more samples to segments expected to contribute, but it remains a ray-marching, multi-evaluation process rather than a constant-time surface lookup. The implication is that the original formulation is well matched to offline per-scene optimization and high-quality view synthesis, but its basic rendering path is too expensive for interactive visualization without changing sampling, storage, or the visibility pipeline. assertions.source_quote: A second limitation is scale and aliasing. Foundational NeRF samples a scene with a single ray per pixel, so it can produce blurred results when training images observe content at nonuniform scales and aliasing or jagged artifacts when test views are distant. Simply casting multiple rays per pixel is a direct supersampling remedy, but in NeRF it multiplies an already large MLP-query cost and is generally impractical outside offline rendering. Mip-NeRF's scale-aware conical frustums and later explicit mip voxel grids are evidence that this is a real limitation of point-ray sampling; they also show that anti-aliasing and real-time deployment may require separate architectural changes. assertions.source_quote: A second limitation is scale and aliasing. Foundational NeRF samples a scene with a single ray per pixel, so it can produce blurred results when training images observe content at nonuniform scales and aliasing or jagged artifacts when test views are distant. Simply casting multiple rays per pixel is a direct supersampling remedy, but in NeRF it multiplies an already large MLP-query cost and is generally impractical outside offline rendering. Mip-NeRF's scale-aware conical frustums and later explicit mip voxel grids are evidence that this is a real limitation of point-ray sampling; they also show that anti-aliasing and real-time deployment may require separate architectural changes. assertions.source_quote: The continuous density field is a rendering representation, not by itself an unambiguous explicit surface reconstruction. NeRF is supervised through rendered color, and later analysis identifies a shape-radiance ambiguity: view-dependent radiance and inferred geometry can interact so that image fidelity does not necessarily determine one unique geometric explanation. This matters when the desired output is a mesh, accurate normals, animation, or manipulation rather than a novel-view image. Methods that normalize view dependence or use explicit surface and texture models target that geometry ambiguity, but they add assumptions or components not present in the original color-supervised volume-rendering setup. assertions.source_quote: View-dependent color is both a capability and a modeling boundary. Allowing RGB to depend on position and viewing direction lets foundational NeRF represent non-Lambertian effects such as specular highlights, but highly shiny scenes can contain quickly changing appearance and reflections of nearby content that a single outgoing-radiance MLP may model only at substantial network cost. Reflection-ray methods address this by tracing additional rays through the field and decoding traced features with a smaller network. That evidence should be read as a limitation of the original appearance model under strong specularity, not as a failure of density-based volume rendering in general. assertions.source_quote: The original NeRF also has a data-regime limitation: it optimizes a separate MLP for each scene from posed training images. It is not a feed-forward model that reconstructs an unseen scene from one image, and the basic formulation assumes camera poses are available for photometric supervision. PixelNeRF and conditional or diffusion-distilled systems introduce image features, learned cross-scene priors, or generated virtual views to operate from one or a sparse set of inputs. These methods relax the original data requirement, but they change the learning problem and should not be interpreted as the same per-scene optimization result. assertions.source_quote: Memory and hardware compatibility create a separate trade-off when NeRFs are accelerated. Caching or baking a continuous field into sparse voxels can improve rendering speed, but it raises storage or GPU-memory use; SNeRG's precomputed sparse grid, for example, accelerates deferred rendering yet still ray-marches volumetric textures and requires significant GPU memory. MobileNeRF instead moves visibility to textured polygons and z-buffer rasterization so commodity graphics pipelines and mobile GPUs can be used. These are deployment solutions, not free speedups of the original MLP: they alter the representation store and often require baking or a deferred shader. assertions.source_quote: Large scenes intensify both computation and organization costs. A single monolithic ray-marched field does not naturally map to the culling, level-of-detail, and rasterization mechanisms used for urban-scale interactive graphics. Systems such as UE4-NeRF partition scenes and combine optimized mesh-like proxies with game-engine rasterization, while deformable neural mesh primitives seek rasterization efficiency and lower peak memory for urban rendering. Their speed and memory claims depend on those primitives, partitioning, level-of-detail, and engine integration; they do not establish that the unmodified foundational NeRF has the same scalability. Systems such as UE4-NeRF partition scenes and combine optimized mesh-like proxies with game-engine rasterization, while deformable neural mesh primitives seek rasterization efficiency and lower peak memory for urban rendering. assertions.source_quote: Architecture choice also involves downstream trade-offs beyond average rendering quality. Plain MLPs provide a continuous coordinate field with comparatively clear functional structure, whereas hash tables, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, tri-planes, and hybrid encodings can train or render faster but may have less clear geometric meaning or different memory profiles. PVD's any-to-any distillation and Hyb-NeRF's coarse-to-fine hybrid encoding are responses to this fragmentation: practitioners may convert or combine representations for editing, training speed, rendering speed, or memory. The limitation is that no single store in the selected evidence dominates all of these objectives simultaneously. assertions.source_quote: Taken together, these limitations should be attributed to specific parts of the pipeline rather than used as a blanket claim that neural radiance fields are unsuitable. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Large scenes intensify both computation and organization costs. A single monolithic ray-marched field does not naturally map to the culling, level-of-detail, and rasterization mechanisms used for urban-scale interactive graphics. Systems such as UE4-NeRF partition scenes and combine optimized mesh-like proxies with game-engine rasterization, while deformable neural mesh primitives seek rasterization efficiency and lower peak memory for urban rendering. Their speed and memory claims depend on those primitives, partitioning, level-of-detail, and engine integration; they do not establish that the unmodified foundational NeRF has the same scalability.
